SCORPION July 8th—Albert Hort a.'
ASTORIA, July 8th—Albert Hoyt, a long-sheman, and a married man, was examined this afternoon in the Justices' Court, charged with rape on Addie Cook, aged 9 years, the daughter of an actress in Hill's Varieties. The deed was committed yesterday evening. The child was cruelly lacerated. The mother discovered the atrocity at a late hour, and the child divulged the name of the villain, who was shortly after arrested by the police. At a late hour a large crowd assembled around the jail, and a rope was prepared for hanging the criminal. Chief Barry was requested to conduct the prisoner to the child for identification, and informed that she was dying. Suspecting their design he refused, and set guard on the jail. This afternoon Cook, stepfather of the child, was in the Police Court armed with a revolver. As he had expressed his intention to shoot the prisoner he was watched and disarmed. Shortly after entering the Court-room the prisoner plead guilty to the charge, and was bound over in $5,000 and then hurried back to prison. Outrages of a similar kind are getting too common, and from present indications Hoyt is very likely yet to be summarily dealt with by Judge Lynch.

OREGON.
Albert Hoyt Charged with Rape — Great Danger of His Being Lynched.

Astoria, July 9.—Albert Hoyt, a longshoreman, and a married man, was this morning in the Justice Court, charged with rape on Addie Cook, aged 9 years, the daughter of an actress in Hill's Varieties. Cook, the stepfather of the child, was in the Police Court armed with a revolver. As he had expressed his intention to shoot the prisoner he was watched and disarmed shortly after entering the Courtroom. The prisoner plead guilty to the charge, and bound over in the sum of $5,000. He was then hurried back to prison to avoid lynching, of which there is great danger.

Advices from Portland.

PORTLAND, August 15th.—The new Department commander, General Nelson A. Miles, in the course of a conversation to-day, said it was the intention of the Government to maintain Vancouver as a large and permanent military establishment, and that at no very distant time the whole military reservation will be required for the use of the Government, and would necessitate the closing up of all the county roads now traversing the Government reserve.

Captain T. J. Stump, who died Saturday very suddenly at Ainsworth, came to Oregon in 1862 from California, where he had been employed by the California Steam Navigation Company as Captain and pilot on the Sacramento river and San Francisco bay. Since then he was in the employ of the Oregon Steam Navigation Company, and its successors, most of the time on the upper Columbia and Snake rivers. He was a very competent steamboat man, and a good citizen. He leaves a wife and three children.

Albert Hoyt, under sentence to the penitentiary for twenty years, charged with rape, and William Sweeney, two years for larceny, made an unsuccessful attempt to break from the city jail this morning. They cut a hole through the floor, and getting under, attempted to crawl out, but were captured by the jailer.

L. Haspoole, a sporting man of Albany, while under the influence of liquor last night, was robbed of $900 in gold coin. A man named T. J. Ankeney was arrested on a charge of stealing the money. To-day he had a preliminary examination, and was held to await the action of the Grand Jury. In default Ankeney was committed.

A German named Antoine Packinger, aged 57 years, shot himself in the month yesterday at Albany. The ball passed through the check and lodged in the neck. Packinger is still alive, but it is thought will die. He is a stranger, and gives as a reason for the attempt on his life that he was destitute and friendless.

Two stables, belonging to M. Heffron, in Linn county, were destroyed by fire this morning. Loss, $1,000; no insurance. The fire was the work of an incendiary.

Two dwellings, belonging to C. P. Ellwanger and A. Alden, situated in the southwest portion of the city, were destroyed by fire this afternoon. Ellwanger's loss is $2,000; insurance, $1,000. Alden's loss is $600; insured for $250.

WHOLESALE POISONING.
WHOLESALE POISONING.

GALVESTON, Aug. 27.—A News Dallas special says: News has reached the city that Mrs. Smith, a widow living near Kaufman, and several members of her family and some tenants, ten in all, were poisoned by eating cooked peaches containing arsneic. Medical assistance was summoned, but at last reports there was little hope of therecovery of any of the injured parties.

KILLED BY OUTLAWS.

SILVERTON, Col. 26—Last night D. C. Ogsbury, city marshal, was killed by two roughs, Burt Wilkinson and Dyson Eskridge. The whole town was aroused and the murderers will be lynched if captured. Eskridge is a notorious desperado and large rewards are offered for his arrest for other crimes.

AN IOWA STORM.

DES MOINES, Aug. 27.—A tremendous wind storm passed over Carroll county, eight miles from Carroll city, leveling grain stacks, corn, etc. A son of Adam Schleisman, 13 years old, driving a reaper was blown from his seat alighting in front of the reaper and the sickle ripped his body open from the throat to the abdomen. Death was instantaneous. The storm lasted five minutes.

THROUGH A BRIDGE.
Des Moines, Aug. 27—This morning the early west bound freight train on the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy road fell through a burnt bridge over Cedar creek three miles west of Albia and ten cars and their contents were burned up. The engineer and fireman jumped and saved themselves. A brakeman was fatally injured.

CHILD BURNED TO DEATH.
Des Moines, Aug. 27—Yesterday evening four miles north of Greenfield, Adair county the 3-years-old child of Rush Piper set fire to a strawstack while playing around it, and was burned to death.

LYNCHED.
Special Correspondence of The Chicago Tribune,
Rico, Colo., Sept. 10. About 9:30 last Sunday evening the closing scene of a most thrilling tragedy was played at Silverton, thirty-five miles northeast of here. Some days before a promiscuous shooting-match had occurred in a saloon several miles north of Durango, on the Durango and Silverton toll-road. During the molle the salookeeper was killed, but no one know who fired the fatal shot. Hert Wilkinson and a "coon" named Jim Catrin, both of whom had figured prominently in the row, immediately made themselves scarce, and shortly afterwards turned up, in company with Dison Eskridge, on the streets of Silverton. Eskridge, who had been here for some time attending to mining interests, had started for Durango the morning of the day on which the shooting occurred. It is claimed that he was not present when the saloonkeeper was killed. The Marshal of Silverton, Clate Ogsbury, attempted to arrest the party, and was

KILLED ALMOST INSTANTLY, living only long enough to state that Wilkinson was the one to whom he owed his death.

The three at once fled, but nearly 100 men were upon their track within a few minutes. Catrin was caught the next day and lodged in the Silverton Jail, from which he was taken the same evening and lynch law most effectively dealt out to him. A reward of $5,500 was offered for the delivery, dead or alive, to the Sheriff of San Juan County, of Wilkinson and Eskridge. The latter is still at liberty. The former was captured by the notorious Ike Stockton, for whom Wilkinson would have risked his life at any time, of which fact Stockton was perfectly aware. The following account of the capture was given by Mrs. Flora W. Pyle, the sister of Wilkinson, who resides at Castle Rock Springs. The statement of Mrs. Pyle was taken verbatim by a special reporter of the Dolores News, and is the only true and accurate account yet given:

"My brother (A. W. Wilkinson) and Dison Eskridge came to our house at 12 o'clock at night on Sunday. They knocked at the door gently, and I answered the call, asking who was there. The answer was, 'Bert.' When I recognized Bert his first words were: 'Flora, we are awful hungry, but have you got anything that will fit Dison's feet; he is barefooted. He then asked if I had anything cooked. I gave them a lunch, which they ate outdoors. They did not enter the house during the time they were hereabouts.

IKE STOCKTON

had arrived here in the evening preceding that night, and was then sleeping in the house across the way. I told the boys of this, when they seemed to be overjoyed, and expressed a desire to see him immediately. Stockton was then sent for, and when he came over to see them he remarked: It is very cold this evening! His teeth were chattering, he was trembling, and I suppose he made this remark to hide the true cause of his nervousness, which was that his conscience smote him for the treachery he was practicing toward his friend, whom he intended to deliver up to be hanged for money's sake. Stockton had been to my house for supper, and returned for breakfast, at the request of a friend, Mr. Welfoot, who had the hospitality of our home. I had made every arrangement for the boys to get horses and provisions with which to continue their travels. I aided in their escape (so far as they went), and if it be criminal I would not regret it, for Bert was my brother, and Dlson his sworn friend. Had I not done as I did, I would feel that I were inhuman. Bert asked who was blamed for the shooting, but did not deny or acknowledge that he killed the Marshal, as he could not know. Mr. Stockton said when he came to our house that night that he had heard that a party would arrive from Silverton, and that he

HAD COME TO WARN THE BOYS, if here. After the boys had eaten their lunch, I was conversing with them at the door. Dlson said to tell his brother Arg that he and Bert would go to their brother, Dow Eskridge, and from his place on to the plains. I am told by witnesses to their arrangement that Stockton tried to have the boys separate, saying that they could escape much easier in that way. They had horses, and provisions to lust them four or five days. They both said while here that when they had reached a place where they could go to work and behave themselves they would do so, and in the future live and act honorably.

"Stockton, when asked in to breakfast, said he was not hungry, but sat down to the table and ate a hearty breakfast, conversing freely all the while about matters of small consequence, and wanted Mr. Welfoot to go to Farmington with him. He had a great deal to say about his living in dread of the law, and said many of his friends had advised him to leave this country and change his name, etc. The manner in which STOCKTON, AS A COMBADE, CAPTURED BERT has caused him to say much to vindicate his treacherous action. He seems to think he has a statement to make to all he meets, separately and collectively. He says that Bert owed him $19 and refused to pay it.

"Bert told me after his capture that he and Dlson went to the place agreed on with Stockton the night they were here, and Stockton and Cook came to them in the morning. Stockton said he would have to go to the Florida after fresh horses. He left Bert and Cook and took Dlson with him. He was gone till 3 o'clock in the afternoon and returned without Dlson. He told Bert that Dlson and Arg were to meet them five miles below with fresh horses. Bert got up and left his pistol on a blanket on which he had been lying. The horse was five or six yards from him, and as he started for him Stockton jumped in between him and his pistol and told him to throw up his hands. Bert did so, laughing, thinking it was a joke; but seeing Stockton's face the truth commenced to dawn on him, and he said: 'Ike, do you mean it?' to which Stockton replied: 'Yes, I do mean it. Money is what makes men in this country. Bert said: 'You've got the drop on me. Ike, but I'd rather you'd kill me.' Stockton promised him he'd never be turned over without something to defend himself with."

AFTER HIS CAPTURE

he was kept under a strong guard at Animal City until Saturday, when he was turned over to the Sheriff of San Juan County, who took him to Silverton and lodged him in jail. He was accompanied by his sister, who remained in Silverton till Sunday. It was no doubt, due to her presence that he was no lynched Saturday night. She was informed Sunday that he would be hanged whether she remained in town or not, and that if she went her brother's body would be sent to her. Between 9 and 10 o'clock Sunday evening a party of masked men broke into the jail, took Wilkinson out, and made summaries preparations for launching him into the green beyond. Up to the last moment he showed the utmost fortitude, and died "the gamer of the game." As the preparations neared completion, he took the rope in his hands and with the remark

"BOYS, I'LL HELP YOU ALL I CAN," adjusted the noose about his own neck, and after expressing his regrets that he could shoot Stockton before going, "who," he said, "sold me for my blood-money," and requesting that his body should not be photographed, kicked the chair upon his stoop from under, and paid in full the debt crime which he had incurred.

STATE NEWS.
The Utes have gone.

The Utes have gone.

Longmont has several telephone lines.

The steel works at Pueblo have started up.

Ouray is to have water works at a cost of $20,000.

The Abbott opera at Denver was a complete success.

The cars will be running into Villa Grove by the 25th.

The Republic is a new daily newspaper in Colorado Springs.

Ore thieves are abroad in Leadville. Three were recently arrested.

The dog killer of Denver has killed about 5,000 canines so far this year.

Denver now has a paid fire department and twenty additional police men.

The mountain range near Buena Vista was covered with snow last week.

The gross earnings of the D. & R. G. for the past eight months were $3,720,335.

The best portion of the Uncompah-gre valley has already been taken up by settlers.

President Palmer, of the D. & R. G. has given $8,000 to the building fund of Colorado college.

The Summit County Journal is a new paper published at Breckenridge by J. Cooper Fincher.

The "Black Kid" and Burt Wilkinson, murderers of Marshal Ogsbury, of Silverton, are dead. Lynched.

A grey eagle was shot recently in the San Juan country which measured six feet from tip to tip of wings.

The Journal of Commerce is a new paper in Denver published by well-known business and newspaper men.

C. S. Triplett is the editor and publisher of a democratic paper at Maysville called the Chaffee County Democrat.

Governor Pitkin has contributed $100 to the fund being raised for the family of the murdered Major Carpenter.

The second annual meeting of the Woman's Christain Temperance Union will convene in Colorado Springs on the 28th.

Perry White sowed eight acres in winter wheat in Boulder county last fall which yielded forty-four bushels to the acre.

James G. Wright died in August at Fort Collins with symptoms of the Asiatic cholera, caused by drinking ditch water.

It is estimated that the total assessment of Colorado this year will be $93,000,000 an increase over last year of $19,000,000.

Wm. Whitson and Chas. Keyser quarreled in Chama on the 9th and in order to settle their difficulties fought a duel at ten steps and both were killed.

The two desperados who rode through Gunnison City a few days ago firing off revolvers, one shot striking Reuben Thom in the leg, have been arrested.

The democrats of the Seventh judicial district have nominated Thos. C. Brown, of Gunnison, for judge and H. C. Montague, of San Juan, for district attorney.

The Saguache Chronicle reports a wedding and probable murder at a Mexican settlement near there last week, on the same day. The bride-groom stabbed a man with whom he had a difficulty.

Geo. Butterworth was knocked down and then kicked under the chin, the blow breaking his neck and instantly killing him, by 'Chief' Lowe, near Red Cliff last week. Both were railroad laborers.

The democrats of Chaffee county have nominated the following ticket: Clerk and recorder, J. H. Johnson; sheriff, W. A. Rogers; treasurer, E. B. Jones; assessor, T. J. Ebrhart; coroner, Dr. A. E. Wright; surveyor, Geo. Bethune; superintendent of schools, Jos. Hollister; and county commissioner, W. H. Champ.

LATEST NEWS
—A London dispatch states that France and England have agreed on an Anglo-French military commission for the reorganization of the Egyptian army so as to prevent future annoyance to either nation.

—John W. Brooks, of Boston, the famous railroad manager, died at Heidelberg, Germany, in his 63d year. He constructed the Boston and Maine road, negotiated the purchase of the Michigan Central by Boston capitalists, built various sections of the Burlington road, and was Chairman of the Hoosac tunnel commission.

—Dr. Lugenbeel, a brother of Mrs. Christiancy, sent a formal challenge to the ex-Minister, which was declined, and a warrant asked for. The cause was reflections upon her testimony in the divorce suit.

—Portions of Iowa, Minnesota, Michigan and Nebraska, were visited by a slight snow-fall on the 16th of September.

—The New York Prohibitionists have nominated a full ticket for State officers, to be voted for at the November election.

—The value of buildings erected in Chicago, so far this year, approximates $10,275,000.

—Wheat along the Canadian Pacific road in Manitoba is said to average fully twenty-five bushels per acre, oats sixty and barley thirty.

—The Department of Agriculture reports the general average of the potato crop in the seven chief States at 68.

—Dr. Hutchinson, of Fulton county, Ark., went down into a well on his premises for the purpose of cleaning it out, and was overcome by foul air. A neighbor, while in the act of descending to his assistance, fell to the bottom of the well and broke his neck. A second neighbor descended the deadly pit and he, too, was overcome by and died from the effects of the foul gases. A number of persons, attracted by the frantic cries of Mrs. Hutchinson, gathered at the spot, and the bodies of the three dead men were taken from the well. To cap the climax of the horror, Mrs. Hutchinson has gone crazy with grief.

- Nearly $150,000 worth of property has been swept away by fire at East Rome, N. Y.

- A west-bound train from Vicksburg, Miss., ran off the track near Edwards' Depot. A sleeping-car, a passenger car and a Superintendent's car were wrecked. Many passengers were injured, six rather seriously.

- Bert Wilkinson, who during the past year killed no less than three men, was lynched at Silverton, Col.

- A negro woman was roasted alive at Dyke's Mills, La., by a mob of citizens, for having murdered two little children.

- The residence of Mrs. Jane Shiers, near Gastonia, N. C., was blown up by dynamite while she was absent. Charles Deplace, a discarded paramour, is believed to have perpetrated the deed, in the hope of extinguishing a rival.

THE CANNELTON COAL MEN.
Another Dispatch From the Seat of War
From the Colonel in Command.
The Register of yesterday contained
Another Dispatch From the Seat of War
From the Colonel in Command.

The Register of yesterday contained all the information accessible in regard to the strike at Cannelton, which information had been furnished exclusively to its reporter. Only one telegram was received yesterday by the Governor and this we give as follows:

CHARLESTON, November 17.

Gor. J. B. Jackson:

I went to Cannelton to-day. The Sheriff and Prosecuting Attorney believe there will be trouble and the Sheriff has summoned the Hawk's Nest Rifles to Cannelton to preserve the peace and has telegraphed Col. Appleton to have other companies ready in case of need. I directed Col. Appleton to notify company commanders to be ready for orders and himself to go to Cannelton to see what might be needed. I did not modify your orders to St. Clair.

D. L. RUFFNER.

There is now a strong probability that there will be a settlement of the matter without any further show of hostilities. Some of the miners who are engaged in the strike are men of education, and it is said they are opposed to the manner of resisting the employment of other miners now being resorted to by some of the more impetuous of their ranks, and are willing to leave the adjudication of their affairs to the arbitrament of joint committees. If the ideas of these men are followed out the necessity for "troops" will be obviated.

If on the contrary, the interference with the operations of the mines is persisted in by the strikers, the Governor will afford every facility to insure the maintenance of order, and protect the operators of the mines in their rights.

coal-valley-coal-valley-1881-11.A4:
The Alarming Reports
of lawlessness in the Kanawha mining regions, that have been lately telegraphad to the papers, led your correspondent to make a special visit to the scene of action. The facts may be summarized: At Coal Valley about 500 men employed in soft coal mines have been on a strike. They would not work themselves, and did all they could, short of violence, to dissuade others from doing so. The operators brought negroes from Virginia to take their places. The first batch were dissuaded from work by the striking miners. The troops were then called for. The peace was not broken nor was there any sign of trouble beyond the power of the civil authorities to control. The officers themselves admitted this, and I think the people generally regard the calling for troops as premature, and a serious mistake on the part of the Fayette authorities. The demand once made, the Governor could do nothing but comply.

The Question at Issue
between the miners and their employers is one not easily settled. The operators sell their coal to the railroad company, getting ninety-five cents per long ton, or less than three and a half cents per bushel. They pay the miner sixty-two and a half cents per ton; and to the land owner a royalty of fourteen cents per ton, besides ordinary running expenses, making the coal stand in the cars nearly what they get for it, and leaving them as margin nothing but the profits on the goods sold to the miners from the stores. To pay the increase of fifteen cents demanded by the miners is impossible unless the railroad should concede an advance on the price paid the operator. The miner, on the other hand, claims that he cannot live at sixty-two cents per ton. When employed he can make, one day with another, about one dollar and fifty cents per day net. Out of this he must pay six dollars a month house rent, and provide for his family. This he might do if the work were constant, but the railroad will not furnish cars to the operator more than half the time.

So the miner must live a year on the proceeds of six months' work. Lately there was an advance of fifty cents per ton in market, and the miners insist this advance should be divided between the railroad, the operator and the digger. The C. & O. railroad insists, however, upon taking all, on the ground as alleged that heretofore it has been carrying coal at a loss in order to keep the mines running and give the men work.

I think this railroad should be relieved from duty as a philanthropist. A law restricting railroads to their business as common carrier, preventing them from speculating in the industrial products along their line and requiring them to furnish cars for all freight that offers, would seem to be about the proper remedy. It would at any rate simplify matters by eliminating the railroad from the complication, allowing the operator to hunt his own market and make his own contracts, and leave him and his miners free to adopt a sliding scale adjusted with reference to the market price of coal. Such a scale is adopted at Campbell's Creek, where millions of bushels of coal are mined without a word of dispute and without a day's strike.

Policies.

You hear more of politics in this county than anywhere else in this section. In former years the Third district had no other interest save in politics, parties, conventions and candidates.

From every neighborhood the small fry politicians went out to disport themselves in the pool of which Charleston was the center, and the District the circumference. It is not so now.

At college the class in rhetoric used to have as an example of anti-climax the following poetical lines:
“Roll on, thon Connecticut, long hast thou ran,
Bringing shad to South Hadley and freedom to man.”

Still roll the Guyandotte and Kanawha as of old, from the solitude of sang-bearing wildernesses, and the sublime mysteries realms whence come forth vast Democratic majorities, dread, fathomless, inscrutable. But statesmanship now seldom troubles these blue waters with its canoes and keels.

“Shad to South Hadley and freedom to man,” no longer form the sole burden of the country’s business. The talk is of trade and telegraphs; mines and mills; timber and tobacco, and railroads and the restless elements of practical civilization. Here in Mason the idea that office-holding is the chief end of man still has its tenacious hold upon the public mind, but even here I can see something of an abatement of the popular passion. Time was when Mason county could furnish the material for both State tickets and have a surplus left for Congressional purposes.

Now, if she can have Barbee on the Independent ticket for Congress, with Hogg or Schon to oppose him as the Democratic nominee, with the understanding that some other Mason statesman is to succeed Davis in the Senate, and John English can have reserved for him a seat on the Supreme Bench, I think even Mason’s appetite would be sated.

WEST VIRGINIA.
THE MINERS' TROUBLE IN THE KANDAWA VALLEY.
An Interview With the Prosecuting Attorney of Fayette County-The Cause of the Trouble and What is Needed to Remedy it.
A WHEELING AUTHOR'S TWO NOVELS.
Specia Correspondence of the Register.
WASHINGTON December 12, 1907

A WHEELING AUTHOR'S TWO NOVELS.

Specia Correspondence of the Register.

WASHINGTON, December 12.—I met Mr. J. W. St. Clair, the prosecuting attorney of Fayette county, here to-day, and had considerable talk with him concerning the recent miners troubles in the Kanawha section. He is a middle aged, muscular and plucky looking individual, and seems like the right sort of a man to hold his own in a rough community. He said he thought the troubles in his section of the State had been settled for the time being, and had been settled in the only way in which it was possible to settle them. "It had come to be a mere question," he said, "whether the coal operators in the coal valley should control their own property or not; and as the miner's association was so constructed and extended that trespassers could not be punished under the present laws, the only way to get along was to meet

Force With Force

when trespasses were attempted. I advised Wyant, one of the larger operators in the valley, whose employees were about to be interfered with, that if he posted his place and warned the strikers not to come on it, that he would have the right to keep them off, and, if necessary, shoot and drag them off. "Well," said Wyant, "if that is the law, I'll keep 'em off," and getting a box of shotguns he put them in the hands of trusted employees, and has been free from annoyance ever since.

The Faulkners, who have mines in the same neighborhood, pursued the same course and with the same success, and Eugene Dana, who manages the Campbell's creek mines, a little lower down, get along comfortably by exhibiting similar nerve when threatened.

As to the Recent Trouble

at Strain's, he said, the strike was ostensibly made against the railroad in the first instance, the men admitting that the operators could not pay the advance asked without an increase in the price paid for coal by the C. & O. agency. The mine owners used every effort to get an advance, and when they were unsuccessful offered their former miners a chance to go back to work at the old prices before trying the experiment of importing colored miners. The old hands refused to take hold or allow any one else, and got the first set of negroes imported to stop, by threatening their lives if they did not, and offering to take care of them if they did. It was in this part of the transaction that the women figured, assembling at the pitmouth with pans and sticks, their husbands and friends meanwhile congregating in the vicinity to the

Number of Several Hundred.

"You may not think a demonstration by women would amount to much," added St. Clair, "but when you come to tackle a crowd of square-built English and Welsh women, some of whom can whip an ordinary man in a fist-fight without any trouble, it is not so trifling a thing." Anyhow it was enough, aided by the backing at hand, to scare out the new hands, and some of them craw'ed out through the air-course in preference to facing the mob. The next lot brought on were negroes of the same class, and it was a mere question of protecting or abandoning the owners in their right to work them. The strikers, numbering about 400, were waiting for the negroes at the station, and the county officials

Were Powerless

to assert their authority and protect the new hands. The Sheriff, Tyree, is a man of good courage and equal good sense. He knew he could get no pass sufficient to bear him out in the immediate neighborhood. He had the right to call on the nearest organized military company or battalion for assistance without consulting the Governor, but he thought the authority of the Chief Executive would have weight, and the Governor promptly gave him permission to use such authority for the purpose of doing what he had a right to do without it. That was all there was of it. We got two companies on the ground and guarded the negroes from intrusion a couple of days until the strikers saw that they could not intimidate them into leaving and dispersed.

"Isn't there any other way to meet these troubles when they arise?"

"Not at present, and under similar circumstances. We have no proper legislation on the subject of trespass, and you can't very well go back to the common law proceeding on an information before a magistrate. Besides, with the influence of the Miner's Union against you, it is almost impossible to get testimony from witnesses who have full knowledge of facts. You have no idea of the class you have to deal with. There is not so much trouble with the Americans, Irish and negroes, but the English and Welsh contain a good many troublesome characters who work up most of the devilment. If I have received one anonymous letter

Threatening My Life,

I have had 20. The day I shot the negro who was endeavoring to escape, I was threatened by a mob, and at other times I have had to get out shooting irons in order to assert my right to stay where it was my plain duty to be. What is needed to put an end to this state of things, is legislation like that which stopped similar troubles in Pennsylvania. I know there will be some trouble in getting it, because there are always some members who will not act as they know they ought to act, for fear of losing a few votes, but the present Legislature is an exceptionally good one, and there have been, I think, enough exhibitions of the situation in our section to induce prompt and proper action by the two houses this winter.

Charlie Russell, whose industry helped to break up the Wheeling Standard, and who subsequently made considerable reputation as a historical novelist, lives here now, and he told me, yesterday, that he had a couple of brand new novels nearly ready for the press. The scene of one of them is laid in Wheeling, and the heroine, a fragile daughter of the southland, breaks one of her lower limbs in the second chapter. The hero, a young physician, is called in, but by an unfortunate mistake, "sets" the wrong limb. This naturally brings about an estrangement, but mutual explanations and corrections follow, and what might have been a fatal separation glides peacefully into a happy and enduring union. I do not know that I have reproduced the incidents exactly, but these will suffice to show what an inviting field the new Commonwealth is for the worker in moral fiction. Mr. Russell stated to me, what has been called to my attention by other novelists, that the absence of a proper international copyright law is gradually deterring many authors on this side of the waters from further attempts at works of fiction. Under the cheap system now in vogue of reproducing not only the standard but the best of the ephemeral foreign literature of the day in the cheap Seaside and Franklin Square editions, atten and twenty cents a volume, an American novel which is put upon the market at a dollar a volume stands very little chance of general circulation.

columbus-hill-baltimore-1881-08-20.A2: A boot-BLACK KILLED IN THE PRESENCE OF A POLICEMAN.—Columbus Hill, a colored bootblack, was fatally stabbed Saturday night at the Hanover Street Market, in Baltimore, by Daniel Sullivan. The murderous act was apparently unprovoked and wanton, and was done almost in the presence of a policeman, who stood near by. Hill was taken to a police station, where he soon expired. Sullivan was promptly arrested and imprisoned. He is a notorious character, having been frequently arrestee for larceny and other offences.
columbus-hill-baltimore-1881-08-20.A3:
COLD-BLOODED MURDER, Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
BALTIMORE, Md., Aug. 21.—The vicinity of the Hanover Market in South Baltimore was the scene of another terrible tragedy at a late hour last night. Singularly, the murder was committed within a few yards of the spot marked by the bloody death of one week ago. This time a white man was the murderer and an inoffensive colored man the victim, while last week it was just the opposite. It was near midnight, and time for the closing of the market, when the colored man, Columbus Hill, in passing along the crowded street opposite the market-house, brushed against Daniel or "Danny" Sullivan, a notorious South Town rough. Hill apologetically remarked, "Beg pardon, boss, I didn't mean it," but, unbeeding the polite apology, the white villain drew a knife and plunged the sharp blade to the hilt in the colored man's breast, the stool piercing the heart. Hill fell heavily to the pavement and expired almost immediately. Sullivan throw the bloody knife into the street, and darted away into the crowds of people about the market. The cry of murder, which was raised, drew nearly a thousand negroes to the scene, as at that late hour of market-night, and in that part of the city, the place is always strung with colored people. Several police were almost immediately in pursuit of the murderer, and as soon as the crowd of negroes learned that one of their color had been murdered in cold blood by a white man they, too, rushed after the police in chase of the perpetrator of the crime. Sullivan was found in about ten minutes concealed in an alley close by the market, but the officers who made the arrest had to wait until they were reinforced with more men from the Southern District Police Station before they could take the prisoner to the station, so excited was the crowd that followed them threatening revenge and lynching.

MURDERED WITHOUT CAUSE.
BALTIMORE, Md., Aug. 21.—Columbus Hill, a colored boot-black, was fatally stabbed last night, at the Hanover Street Market, by Daniel Sullivan. The murderous act was apparently unprovoked, and was done almost in the presence of a policeman. Hill was taken to a police station, where he soon expired. Sullivan was arrested and imprisoned.

THE NEWS
Of the Day in Pithy Paragraphs.
Domestic.
Domestic.

E. B. Backus, a merchant of Independence, Iowa, went to the grave of his wife and shot himself in the temple.

A corner in January corn is said to have been organized in St. Louis, where the shortage approaches a million bushels.

The result of the pool tournament at New York was, Wahlstrom first prize, Frey second, Morris third, and King fourth.

Vaccination parties are all the style in the best society in New York now. The dread disease has a fair foot hold there now.

H. B. Kelley, editor of the Lima Democrat, died in Washington on Saturday, while visiting the city with the other members of the Ohio Press Association.

Chas. McKnight, one of the editors and proprietors of the Philadelphia Evening News, and formerly connected with the Pittsburgh Evening Chronicle, is dead.

Is the turpentine section of North Carolina, a colored horse-trader named Boyral Bryant, was lynched by parties unknown. He had once escaped conviction for murder.

James French, a brakeman on the Piedmont road, in North Carolina, undertook to dance a jig on top of a moving freight car, but was killed by a covered bridge, near Salisbury.

A playful scuffle between a rough and a gambler, at Bodie, Col., ended by their winding themselves about each other and shooting until one was dead and the other mortally wounded.

An Atlanta, Ga., dispatch says: Carrie Stokes, colored, was murdered last night, the body placed upon a fire, wood pulled around, and the clothing saturated with coal oil. The head and face were horribly burned.

England's army estimates for 1881 foot up the enormous total of $100,000,100. The by jingo policy comes high, but England must have it.

doyral-bryant-fayetteville-1881-01.A3:
THE MURDERER'S REWARD
A Strange Murder Mysteriously Avenged—Sequel of a Midnight Orgle of the Year 1873.

FAYETTEVILLE, N.C., Jan. 21.—About 0 o'clock one bright morning, the 15th day of October, 1873, a little boy ran very excitedly along one of the principal streets of Fayetteville, and, meeting an old and prominent citizen of the town, stopped short and exclaimed, "Mister, there's a dead man lying in Rich Mims' house!" The news was immediately reported at the Sheriff's office, and on his Deputy and assistants hastening to the scene it was confirmed by the spectacle of a ghastly and heart-sickening tragedy. On the one miserable bed of the hut or cabin lay a strange-looking creature, a misshapen negro dwarf, not more than four feet in height, but with a huge head and body. In hight and form he was not unlike the black dwarf of Sir Walter Scott. This was Rich Mims, sunk in the brutish insensibility of a drunken sleep. On the floor, weltering in his blood, with his skull beaten in, dead, and stark, and still, lay a young white man, recognized as Charley Boone. An Investigation elicited the following facts:

This singular dwarf lived in a little house in the southern suburbs of the town, in a lonely spot near the edge of a large mill-pond. On the evening previous to the discovery of the murder two mulattos, Doyle Bryant and Wiley Evans, accompanied by Funny Briggs, a white woman of abandoned character, visited the cabin of Rich Mims and informed the old man that they had an ox head and that he must make them a stew, a delicate dish, for the preparation of which Richard enjoyed an envidia reputation. They were also provided with a quantity of mean whisky, and announced their intention of making a night of it. While the preliminaries for this festive occasion were in preparation and as darkness was closing in Charley Boone, a young man of good family, who had been a faithful soldier in the late War, but a man of dissipated habits, made his appearance. He was invited to take a drink, and perhaps to make himself at home. At any rate, he joined the party at the blazing fire of light wood knots which roared in the old chimney.

"The houses of night crept steadily on. The stars flashed and glittered on the smooth bosom of the great sheet of water outside; all Nature was hushed in rest and silence, broken only by the voice of rude revelry from that solitary hut; but Charley Boone never more stepped forth to the fresh air and bright light of heaven.

"Who "Colonel"—for such was the military title given to the negro dwarf by his admirers—applied himself to the whiskey bottle during the evening, and his frequent potations overcame him. Some time during the night he staggered to his bed, and could only remember that there was a quarrel in the hut, that he saw a man trying to raise himself from the floor, that he heard blows and groans and a woman's voice at a distance calling "Hurry, Wiley! Wiley, Wiley; come out!" Doyle Bryant and Wiley Evans were arrested, and, at the following January term of the Superior Court of Cumberland County, were separately tried for the murder of Charley Boone, when the above with other evidence was adduced. Wiley Evans, one of the prisoners, confessed that there had been a night in Minsk hut, and that he had struck the deceased over the head with a chair. The trial excited great interest, and the court-room was crowded day after day. Through the splendid efforts of his counsel, Mr. T. C. Fuller, now of Rutleigh, Bryant was acquitted, but it was one of the many cases where public opinion refused to nequiesce in the verdict of the jury, and Doyle Bryant has been believed to bear upon him the mark of Calm. He has led a dissolute life ever since, remaining mostly in Fayetteville, and spending his time chiefly in horse-trading, but it seems that he was a marked man.

Now, according to the generally-received rumor here, comes the sequel to the above history and the bloody close of the wretched man's ill-spent life. For seven long years this man has enforced all the rights and liberties of a free citizen, but it seems, according to the general opinion, that retributive justice has at last overtaken him. Some weeks ago a county-fair was held at Clinton, in the neighboring County of Sampson. Bryant left here, to attend this fair with a horse-trader. Whether he left by com-
taken him. Some weeks ago a county-fair was held at Clinton, in the neighboring County of Sampson. Bryant left here to attend this fair with a horse-trader. Whether he left in company with other traders, as some say, or whether he overtook them on the road, is not definitely known, but it seems to be certain that he was seen on the road in company with a crowd of other men, and that all were drunk and bolstered. Bryant, it is said, never reached Clinton, and he has never returned to his home or been seen or heard of by any of his friends. Now comes the intelligence, published in a newspaper in a neighboring county, and in the months of the people of this section, that the body of Bryant has been found hanging by a balter on a tree between Fayetteville and Clinton, the place where the county-fair was held. The two horses, broken down and half starved,—part probably of his trading stock,—were hitched near by, and upon the dead man's back was a plaque, "This is the murderer of Charley Moore."

This report has been denied and reiterated over and over, but this much is certain; Bryant has disappeared. Where is he? His friends have not recovered his body, and do not know of his whereabouts. He had many enemies, and Sampson County is a very lawless neighborhood. Windhur the light of day will ever be let in upon this supposed tragedy I cannot now say. Time may clear up the mystery.

ed-maxwell-durand-1881-11-19.A2:
Another Account.
[Special Telegram to the Globe.]

DURAND, Wis., Nov. 19, via Menomonie.—This place was the scene of great excitement this afternoon, which resulted in the summary execution of the notorious murderer, Ed. Maxwell. Ever since the brutal murder of the Coleman brothers last summer there has been a general talk that if the Williams brothers or Maxwells should be caught they would be promptly mobbed. It was generally expected that if found in the woods they would not be taken alive, but so much time had elapsed that many thought the danger of violence had passed. The prisoner himself imagined he would not be harmed, and so expressed himself on the way, and after his arrival here.

The news of his arrest created a good deal of excitement, and as it became known that he would have his preliminary examination to-day, crowds of people came flocking in at an early hour this morning and all during the forenoon. There was no apparent concert of action, but they seemed to be impelled primarily by curiosity in their coming. As they gathered, however, there was a good deal of quiet talk relative to inflicting summary vengeance and there were plenty who declared themselves ready to tie the rope.

The prisoner was brought into court about 2 o'clock this afternoon and the charge of murder preferred against him. He was perfectly cool and manifested no fear or excitement, evidently calculating that he would be committed to wait trial after the preliminary examination. He presumed too much upon the temper of the crowd. Ever since he has consented to talk at all, he has claimed that he and his brother Lon shot the Coleman brothers in self-defense. This plea was so outrageous that its announcement created great indignation here. When the prisoner stood up and boldly repeated this claim in court, the feeling surpassed all bounds. A rush was made for him, the officers thrown aside, and in a second a ready rope was around his neck, and he was pushed, dragged and thrown out of the window to the court house yard. There seemed to but one sentiment in the crowd, and that was to rid the death of the brute as speedily as possible. No time was lost in dragging him to a convenient tree, and he was strung up, without judge or jury. There was no one who cared to attempt to interfere, and the body was allowed to hang until he was thoroughly dead.

When the deed was fully accomplished there was a general feeling of satisfaction and the crowd quietly dispersed. The universal sentiment here is that he only received his just deserts.

ed-maxwell-durand-1881-11-19.A8:
Fell and Broke Hhis Neck.
St., Paul, Nov. 22.—Nothing had been heard from the Durand scene of the Maxwell lynching until to-day, when the following dispatch was received: The body of Ed. Maxwell was cut down after hanging about half an hour, and an inquest held. The following is the verdict rendered: "Came to his death by falling from the court house steps and breaking his neck." ed-maxwell-durand-1881-11-19.A28: THE Washington Republican and the New York Times (both stalwart journals) are shocked that a white desperado in Wisconsin and a negro ravisher in Ohio, have been lynched. They could not have imagined such outlawry outside of the Southern States.
ed-maxwell-durand-1881-11-19.A29:
[From Same Paper.]
A Daisy of a Reporter.
E. R. Johnstone, reporter of the Pioneer Press, accompanied the officers and Ed. Maxwell from St. Paul last Friday. He evidently went away too soon, as the lynching took place about two hours after he left town. If he comes down with Lon Williams he will probably stay longer. But then we don't see the use of his coming at all. His report of the affair, written in St. Paul, but as if he had been an eye witness of the whole affair, "lays over" anything we have ever heard of. His article is written in as sensational a style as possible and with as little truth as could possibly be worked in. He publishes a confession made by Ed. in the court room, when in fact the murderer made no remarks at all, except to give his name, plead not guilty, and say that he wished to waive examination. He tells of the red and blue shirted lumbermen who did the lynching, when in fact no such persons were in the town. He also lets his imagination loose on the scene in the court room, when in fact the prisoner left the room quietly and was nearly out of the building when seized by his executioners. But it is useless to mention all his lies—we simply deny the whole article, and express our surprise that so enterprising a paper as the Pioneer Press should tolerate such an unmilitated d——n liar.
ed-maxwell-durand-1881-11-19.A32:
The Lynching of Maxwell.
A visitor at Durand on the 19th, who was outside the court house before and during the lynching of Ed. Maxwell, gave the following description of the scene to the Eau Claire Free Press:

I was passing by the court house, on the 19th, at about 2:15. Williams' preliminary examination was supposed to be going on in the upper story, which was jammed with a crowd of 200 or 300 men, women and children. The prisoner was on the south side of the court room, and was pleading "not guilty." Every eye in that vast assemblage was glued on his marble face—pale as death, but firm as adamant. How they hated him! How (here and there in the crowd) the cold glare of savage eyes suggested the awful fate in store for the victim. Yet the greater part of the crowd were unconscious of the plot. They were staring fixedly at the prisoner on the south side of the room. Had they looked from the north windows, out upon a sturdy oak tree about 150 feet from the building they would have seen a rope hanging from a bough projecting about 30 feet above the ground. The end of the rope which dangled from the bough was in the hands of a knot of men waiting and listening under the tree. The rope, which was 300 feet long, passed around the corner of the building to the portico in front, and the other end with a running noose, was in the hands of another knot of men who were waiting to do their part. All was quiet. The gentleman, referred to, had approached nearer in the meantime, and counted no more than twenty men and boys on the portico. Soon the sound of crowding steps was heard inside the building. Williams had waived examination. Court had adjourned. Sheriff Knight and his assistants were leading Williams down stairs to go to the jail, and the crowd was following. The men under the tree got themselves ready to pull their end. The men on the portico who held the noose end of the rope were watching for their prey. The front door opened, and a pistol shot from the crowd inside was heard. Williams came forth, his hands shackled together and one foot free from his iron bonds to allow motion. Like a flash the noose was around his neck. The men at the tree started on a run with the rope. It pulled taut around Williams' throat in a second, and shackled as he was, he was jerked from his feet, and fell on his back with a dull thud, his head being wedged against one of the pillars around which the taut rope passed. A few jerks, and the insensible body, with a great livid bruise on the right temple, rolled down the steps, slid along the ground towards the tree, and rose in the air a corpse. Not a spasm, not a convulsion of his body was seen. The rope was fastened, and the lynchers mixed with the crowd, which had given a yell when the body went up. The officers in the mean time, were not heard from. The crowd, which was noisy and excited, increased, our informant says to over 500, and not a word of sympathy or regret for the fate of Williams was heard. After the body had hung about 20 minutes some officers ventured to cut it down. It was taken into the court house, and at 4:30 was buried in the potter's field. As the body was being removed, the rope was pounded upon and cut to pieces by relic hunters. The gathering slowly dispersed, discussing the matter noisily, yet with decreased excitement, and by five o'clock the usual quiet had settled upon the town.

ed-maxwell-durand-1881-11-19.A37: The New York Times says: 'No story of lynching from the wild Southwestern States can exceed in brutality that of the hanging of a desperado by a Wisconsin mob.' ed-maxwell-durand-1881-11-19.A44: The business portion of the village of Durand, the scene of the Maxwell murder, was destroyed by fire lately. It is said that there were threats made that this would be done unless the lynchers were brought to justice. This seems to be hardly a just retribution although the failure of the state to punish the persons engaged in this crime is a burning disgrace. Smith ordered out the militia to suppress the orgies of a lot of drunken, cowardly Indians, but in Durand, where the law was openly violated and a man deliberately murdered, the act was allowed to pass unnoticed.

MURDER IN NEW MEXICO.
Colonel Charles Potter, of the U. S. Geological Survey, Murdered— The Three Murderers Swung Up By Vigilantes.
Special to the Herald.
Alburquerque, N. M., Jan. 31.—Colonel Charles Potter, of the United States geological survey, who had for some time been collecting statistics for the census bureau, left Alburquerque October 14th, 1880, for the New Placer mining camp. He was seen the next day at Tjera, N. M., traveling toward San Antonita. Since then nothing has been heard of him and his fate had been shrouded in mytery, until a few days ago when Sheriff Armijo, of Bernallillo county, obtained some evidence implicating one Escallero Parera. Measures were at once taken and he was arrested at Isletta, N. M., and brought to this city. He at first denied all knowledge of the affair, but at length confessed that he had been a witness of the crime, though not a sharer in it. The Boom of the Bison.

That the American bison, or buffalo, as it is more familiarly termed, is domed to extinction in time is evident; but that this result will be "a necessary evil" is generally acknowledged among settlers in the Far West. The vast herds of bison that only a few years since roamed over the Western plains afforded wild sport and a large income to the hide-hunters; but as an offset to this it should be remonbored that the buffalo is one of the chief sinns of war with the Indian tribes. Deprive the red man of buffalo, and he cannot, during midwinter especially, carry on a successful raid. From the bison he obtains his provision, robes, and covering. Nothing so barrassed and weakened Bitting Hull and his band, when driven over the Canada border as the absence of buffalo in that region. When the last hards become finally annihilated, nothing remains for the Indian but a semi-civilized and agricultural life. Holding this in view, the extinction of this huge nomad of the plains may be looked forward to, if not with satisfaction, at least with realignation by the sportmen of the land, and especially by the frontiersmen who have suffered so much at the hands of the Sioux and other warlike tribes. At best the bison, as a game animal, possesses merely the qualities of endurance, size and stubbornness,—bearing no more comparison to the elk and moose than does the mule to the thoroughbred.

A Barroom Row in Fernandina Puts the Town in an Uproar- Military Called Out.
Passengers arriving from Florida report that a disgraceful riot occurred in Fernandina on Monday, which resulted in the serious wounding of a negro and the town's being placed for a time at the mercy of a drunken mob. The trouble originated in a barroom quarrel between a negro and a white man, which was adjourned to the street, and attracted a crowd of drunken blacks of both sexes.

In the tumult Policeman Wimberly became involved, but he escaped from the crowd and was joined by his brother and father, who were reported to have stabbed Levi Young, colored, with whom Wimberly had had a difficulty. They started for their home, whither they were followed by the crowd, who threatened to burn their house. The Wimberlys were at length removed to the jail. The mob then threatened to fire it and lynch them. Great excitement prevailed.

Mayor Starke did all he could to restore order and, finally, called on the Fernandina military for aid. He also telegraphed the Governor, and the Jacksonville Infantry were ordered to the town. The troops were stationed at Lyceum Hall, and a guard was placed around the jail. Volunteers came in from other points, but they were not needed. Despite the fact that the town was crowded with colored excursionists, no fears were felt for the safety of the jail or the prisoners after the troops arrived. The ringleaders of the mob will be arrested and dealt with severely.

The senate passed the concurrent resolution concerning the electoral count without any material amendments, and without roll call or division.

The Sacramento valley, Cal., presents the appearance of an inland sea. Numberless houses have been swept away, but fortunately no lives have been lost. For several weeks smallpox has been raging with great fatality at Jefferson, Union county, Dakota, a settlement about 12 miles from Sioux City. CRIMES.
St. Louis, December 20.—Chris Gememhardt, one of the injured in Sunday night's railroad accident near Jefferson City, died yesterday. This is the fourth victim of the accident.

George Mills attempted to commit a rape on Mrs. A. Fink on the highway at Hannibal. He presented a revolver at the lady, who grasped it, and a scuffle ensued, during which the revolver was discharged, the ball taking off part of one of Mrs. Fink's fingers. Mrs. Fink's screams frightened the ruffian, who ran off. On arriving at home she told her husband of the outrage. Fifteen men were soon in search of Mills, and found him at the house of his father. Mills refused to come out and fired at the posse, who thereupon broke down the door and disarmed and overpowered Mills. With difficulty the captors saved Mills from lynching, but he was finally handed over to the authorities. Mills is a hard case.

St. Louis, December 21.—About midnight, Sunday, a man and woman were observed by one Fred. Tompkins, a horse clipper, entering the small yard of the Second Presbyterian church, evidently for improper purposes; and Tompkins (a man noted for his prying, inquisitive disposition) followed and watched them. The man and woman discovered they were watched, and it is supposed Tompkins tried to intercept them as they were coming from the yard, when a pistol was fired and Tompkins fell mortally wounded. The only witness of the deed was C. H. Turner, who declares the woman fired the shot, as the unknown man had gone some distance ahead.

A Negro Desperado's Deadly Work.
MEMPHIS, April 21.—W. F. Beattie, Sheriff of Crittenden county, Ark., was killed this morning near Marion, Ark., twelve miles northwest of this city, while attempting to arrest a negro burglar. Deputy Sheriff Maddox was wounded by the negro murderer, who made his escape. Hayes White is the name of the negro who killed Sheriff Beattie. He had been arrested two days previous while in the act of robbing the safe of Trextor's store, at Crawfordsville, ten miles west of Marion, but made his escape by shooting the colored constable who had him in charge. At the same time he shot a white man named Emmet Sweepstone, who had gone with the officer to assist in taking the prisoner to jail at Marion. Beattie's remains were brought here to-night, and will be forwarded to relatives in Virginia. A large posse of armed men are scouring Crittenden county searching for the murderer, who will be lynched it caught.

BLOODY FIEND.
A Burgling Darky Kills Two Men, Cripples Two Others,
Robs a Dying Victim and Escapes to the Woods.
He Sends Seven Bullets Through He Sends Seven Bullets Through Human Flesh and Bone, Makes No Mistake in His Aim, and is Never Once Shot At.
Strange and Tragic Adventure of
A Murdering Felon.
The entire community in Crittenden county, over the river opposite this city, were startled yesterday morning by the news of the murder of their much respected sheriff, W. F. Beattie, which tragedy occurred near sunrise, not far from Crawfordsville, on the Goodlett plantation, about six miles beyond Marion, the county seat, and some fifteen miles northwest of this city.

Brief mention was made of the tragedy in yesterday's issue of this journal. The details of the strange and unnatural murder came to hand at a later hour, and are as follows:

A yellow man about thirty-two years old named Hays White, reared in Crittenden county and living on the Goodlett farm with his wife and father, has been suspected for some time past of burglarizing various houses near Crawfordsville. Last Monday he broke into the store of W. L. Trexler, and was caught in the act of trying to open the safe. Next day he was examined before a magistrate and committed in default of $1500 bail. Wednesday he started for jail at Marion, six miles distant, under guard of Turner Hendrix, a colored constable, and Emmet Swepstone, a young white man, as assistant. The three were mounted, the prisoner moving in advance. Going two miles of the six without adventure, Hays White, the prisoner, suddenly drew a revolver from beneath his garments, in front of the lower part of his abdomen, and fired upon Hendrix, the bullet boring through the flesh of his arm. He shot again, and another flesh wound through the side brought the officer to the ground. He at once crawled away some distance and hid behind a log.

The prisoner next turned his attention to the white guardsman, Swepstone, and he lost no time about it. Aiming a shot at the officer's head, he tore the top of his hat off, and grazed the scalp. The officer dismounted without delay, perhaps fell off, but managed to tumble on the opposite side from the killer. The latter also dismounted, and on the opposite side from the officer. Each used their respective horses as a fortification. Swepstone's animal being the smallest, that worthy was kept pretty busy dodging about and trying to keep his anatomy covered. The negro trained his pistol on Swepstone, exposed as little of his person as possible, and gradually moved his animated fortress toward the officer. When as close as he wished to get, he ordered Swepstone to drop his weapon. The order was obeyed promptly. The ex-prisoner picked up the weapon, told Swepstone he didn't want to kill him, directed him to mount and move forward, and said he'd take him along for protection. The couple marched, the disarmed officer in the lead. Passing near Hendrix, the fiendish White asked:
"Turner, are you much hurt?"
"Yes," was the reply; "I'm most killed."
"Then I'll finish the job," said White, and he pulled trigger, a bullet crashing through the back of the victim's neck and out of his mouth, which lay next to the earth. Three shots through Hendrix the murderer supposed was enough to fix him, so leaving the man for dead, he moved forward, telling Swepstone that if anyone came in sight and asked questions about the firing, to say that they had been shooting snakes back in the swamp apiece. As odd as it may appear, Swepstone did as directed. Dr. Stull met, and inquired what they had been shooting at. The darky kept his tongue quiet, and his pistol a little to one side, Swepstone said snakes, and the party moved in opposite directions. A little further on, White left the cowed, and disarmed officer, and took the woods. Since then he has not been seen. The badly shot colored constable was yet alive up to the last trip of the ferryboat, but it is believed he cannot possibly survive. The shot through the back of the head did the work.

CAPTURE OF A MURDERER. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
LITTLE ROCK, Ark., April 27.—The negro, Hayes White, who murdered Sheriff Beattie, of Crittenton County, was discovered yesterday morning at daybreak in a cabin ten miles below Augusta by a party of six men from Forest City who were searching for him. The men surrounded the house, but when the door opened and White came out with a pistol in his hand they fell back in confusion, and the desporado walked coolly away. It is said he pulled off his coat and shoes and swam to the opposite side of White River, disappearing in the dense underbrush which lines the banks of that stream. These brakes are almost impenetrable, and it will require the services of bloodhounds to hunt the fugitive from his hiding place. Armed men are swarming to the locality hoping to effect his capture.

LATER.—A special from Augusta announces the capture of White near that place at an early hour this morning. The negro made a desperate resistance, but was overpowered, and is now in trons. He will be taken back to Marion and lodged in fall pending trial. Fears of Judge Lynch are expressed, but it is believed the guards are sufficient to keep the mob at bay.

Yesterday it was announced that Hayes White would be brought to Memphis from Little Rock on the night train. An APPEAL representative went out to meet the train at Blackfish, thirty-three mile siding. At Forrest City a large crowd of persons came on board the train to Lynch White, but Captain McDonald, the conductor, had locked White up in the baggage-car, and told the men that he was in the last car. They went through the train, which started about that time, and they got off. White was brought to Hopefield and across the river to Memphis, and handed over to the police-officers and deputy-sheriffs to be locked up in jail for safe-keeping until to-day, when he will be taken back to Marion for trial.

While coming in on the train the APPEAL reporter obtained from White the following interesting statement of the killing of Turner Hendricks and Sheriff Beattie, his (White's) flight and capture:

Hayes White's Statement.

The trouble was started in the following manner: I was accused of breaking into Mr. Trexler's store, about sundown last Tuesday week, and they sent Turner Hendricks, a colored constable, on Wednesday morning, to arrest me. I had not got up, and was not dressed when he came, but asked him to come in. I went with him, and stood trial. I had proof that I was not in Crawfordsville at the time the store was broken open, but I was put under $1500 bond, which was afterward reduced to $1000. I asked and insisted of the constable to go around with me and try and get the bond, and he refused, saying there was no one in the county but what was on somebody's bond, and so I will have to carry you to jail. I said to him: "As you will not go with me to try and give a bond, I will let you tie my hands, it you will go with me, to see my wife and children before we go to Marion. I will pledge you my word that I will not go further than the fence." He refused, saying: "You might as well put your foot in the road and go to Marion." A young white man, Mr. Sweepston, asked Hendricks what he was afraid of. He said, "Of nothing." I said then to Hendricks, "I will go with you." We started to Trexler's store; when we got there, he ordered me to stop in the road until he got half a pint of whisky. We started for Marion. Whenever we reached any one's house, he would tell Mr. Sweepston to go ahead with me, and before I could get out of hearing I could hear him boasting to the people about carrying me to jail. I made a remark to Sweepston, "Listen to Turner," and said I would speak to him when he came up. Hendricks caught up with us at Gus. Edwards's, and Hendricks gave Edwards a dollar for a horse for me to ride to Marion. We started; Hendricks stopped and boasted at Mrs. Holloway's about carrying me to jail. I said to Mr. Sweepston that I would not hate this so bad if it was not for my wife and children, and being accused of stealing when I was innocent. Sweepston said, "It will not go hard with you if you will get a couple of good boys—lawyers—as I do not expect to appear against you now. Then Hendricks caught up with us again. He came up in a hurry and said to Sweepston, "Let us have some more of that whisky." I said to Hendricks, "I don't think you are treating me right; he asked why, and I said, "because you wouldn't go with me so that I could give a bond; neither would you go with me to see my wife and children." He replied, "Let your wife come to Marion to see you, like other men's wives do," and then I thought of his shooting at me last Christmas and I got mad, but said no more. He (Hendricks) hit my horse and said "walk up." I drew a pistol from my bosom and shoved it against him and fired, and said: "Now, you ride up," but he then fell from his horse. MUMPINS, Tenn., April 20.—Hayes White, the negro desparado who murdered Sheriff W. F. Heattle, of Crittenden County, Ark., and whose capturo was affected recently at Augusta, Ark., was brought to Memphis to-night from Little Rock and lodged in the county jail. DUNDER, Ill., April 29.—A report circulated here yesterday, and published in a Chicago paper, that the body of William Stewart, the missing Algonquin farmer, had been found, proves to be false, no trace of him having been found. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Kelloy, Cashier of the Burlington & Missouri Railroad, was stealing from the Company, and the Auditor yesterday began to check up his accounts. George Walgamuth, agent of the Cleveland, Wabush & Michigan Hallway and a grain-buyer at Treaty Station, was bucked and gagged last night by a gang of four robbers and his safe blown open. Treaty, Ind., April 29. Four masked robbers hold George Walgamuth a prisoner while they took from his safe $300 last night. They led, after gagging him, for the wood. They worked to the word, and it is thought they are an organized oligue.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

SPRINGFIELD, Ill., April 22. A cutting affray occurred here this afternoon in which George Stovons was stabbed in the side by Ira N. Fisko. The knife entered the right side just over the kidney, extending obliquely downward four inches, penetrating the cavity. The man had been drinking together all morning, and the quarrel rose over the question of which should pay for the dinner they had just eaten. Stovons is in a critical condition. Fisko is in jail. Allen and Yancey wore out in the back, and Campbell's throat was cut from ear to ear and his head almost severed from his body. Hunton surrendered to the Sheriff, but was released on a preliminary trial.

White's Story of his Crime.
Hayes White was brought to the
Hayes White was brought to this city last evening and lodged in the county jail during the night. He left this morning by the early ferryboat in charge of officers, for Marion, a large crowd of curious people following him to the river. At Forrest City, on his way here, a crowd boarded the train with the intention of lynching him, but failed in their design, as the conductor had him locked up safely in the baggage car. His story is that after being tried and put under bond for robbing Trexler's store he asked to be allowed to go and see his family, and a chance to give bail, but his requests were refused. The guard, Hendricks, stopped and got a supply of whisky, and at every house they passed, boasted that he was taking a thief to jail. The guard continued to pull at the whisky bottle and abuse him all along the road. At last he (White) grew angry, and drawing a pistol from his bosom, placed it against Hendricks, and fired. Swepston sprang from his horse and White dismounted, using his horse as a barricade. Hendricks, who was not dead, fired at White, and then took refuge behind a log. White walked by Swepston, telling him he did not want to shoot him, and proceeded to fix the colored guard, Hendricks, for good and all. He then demanded Swepston's pistol, told him to mount his horse and go, which he did in a hurry. White then went home, and the next morning, when arranging to leave, saw Sheriff Beattie and Deputy Maddox coming and prepared to defend himself. A moment more and Sheriff Beattie had shoved the door open and snapped his gun at him. The cap failed, and with Swepston's revolver White shot Beattie down, but says he did not know who it was until he had done so. He then stepped to the door and fired at Maddox, who had his gun in shooting position. He then skipped, and avoiding the railroads until he got in the neighborhood of Forrest City, stopped one night there with a negro preacher named Winn. Leaving Forrest City Friday morning, he went through Cotton Plant, crossed Cache river, and stopped at Stewart's place near Augusta, and was finally captured in that neighborhood.

SAFE IN JAIL.

White arrived at Marion about nine o'clock this morning, and was landed within fifty yards of the jail. A large crowd of spectators had collected to witness his debarkation. All was quiet and no demonstration occurred, nor were there any remarks heard among the spectators. White went from the boat to the courthouse escorted by the officers, and when arraigned, said he had no defense to offer, nor did he care to employ lawyers or legal advisers. The court appointed Colonel Lyle and George Phelan to defend him, and set Tuesday next as the time for his trial. After being arraigned, White was quietly conveyed from the courthouse to the jail and locked up, no obstruction being offered by the citizens.

The indications point to a determination on the part of the populace to let the law take its course and to give White a speedy trial.

The colored parson, Winn, who harbored White at Forest City, is in jail at Marion. He went over the river on the early ferryboat at the same time with the prisoner, having an appointment to preach there to-morrow to his colored brethren. He hadn't read the morning paper, hence knew nothing of the public report of his complicity in harboring White until after the Overton landed at Marion. The preacher is not likely to hold forth to his flock to-morrow.

LESTON. May 4. - A Weatherford

GALVESTON, May 4.—A Weatherford special to the News gives further particulars of the fearful wreck of two freight trains at 10 o'clock yesterday forenoon, on the Texas Pacific road 160 miles, and 178 miles west of Weatherford. The accidents were caused by heavy rains, similar to spouts, tearing away two trestle bridges. Engineer W. B. Sanders and Fireman Dyon, of the South bound train, and Engineer Frank Long, and his brother Robert Long, fireman, and Jas. L. Lloyd, brakeman, of the East bound train, were killed. SAFE ROBBERIES.

DETROIT, May 4.—The safe of the county treasurer's office at Bay city was blown open by burglars last night, but only $50 secured, some $1,500 taken in after banking hours fortunately being lodged elsewhere, which the thieves were probably after.

The safe of the store of G. W. Stewart, at Merley, this State, was blown open Sunday night and $150 taken. The job was evidently the work of professionals.

DELIBERATE MURDER.

St. Joseph, Mo., May 4.—Wm. Wise shot and killed Chas. Wilson, just south of the city, at 9 o'clock to-night. They were working for parties who were on the way from Texas to Iowa. Wise was 21 years old and Wilson 18 and they had been cow boys. Wise went to the city this afternoon and bought two revolvers, rode down to the place where the party was camped, called Wilson out of his tent, and, without warning, shot him through the heart, and then fled.

TERRIBLE DESTRUCTION OF LIFE.

London, May 4.—The victims of the explosion on the sloop-of-war Dateral number eight officers and one hundred and thirty-five men killed and three officers and fourteen others saved.

CRUSHED TO DEATH.

LITTLETON, N. H., May 4.—A building connected with the Maplewood hotel property, being raised twenty feet to construct a story under it, fell this afternoon upon a gang of workmen, killing Morris Cheney and Daniel Abbott and seriously injuring several others.

NORTH ADAMS, Mass., May 3.—A smash-up occurred on the Troy & Boston road this morning by which several coaches were thrown down an embankment. All trains so far coming from the West have been delayed. No particulars can be obtained at this time though it is understood there were no fatalities.

A HUMAN FURY.

Hayes White, who to-day atoned his crimes on the gallows, had the reputation of being one of the most daring desperadoes in the Southwest. His history is as remarkable as his deeds. His age was about 40 years, twenty-five of which have been one series of startling adventures and atrocious crimes. Once the property of a Louisiana planter, he burst his bonds by running away. He was captured with bloodhounds and afterward sold to a person who owned a sugar-plantation in Cuba. Before the vessel sailed which was to carry White to a different scene of servitude, he escaped, and remained at large until the War broke his shackles forever. Since then he has spent the greater portion of his life in Arkansas, living in a little cabin and cultivating a few acres of land in Crittenden County. In that time he has been the leader in more than one daring enterprise, always escaping bodily injury, and generally leaving no trace by which the deed could be fastened directly upon him. Murders, robberies, and arsons have been charged upon him repeatedly; and yet, while appearances indicated his guilt, the evidence was not strong enough to entangle him in the meshes of the law.

SHooting A Constable.

The event which cut short his blood-stained career occurred on the night of April 22. On that date a store in the neighborhood of his home was robbed. The thieves secured some money and a considerable amount of valuable goods. White was suspected and arrested. On preliminary examination he was bound over in the sum of $1,000; and, as he could not furnish ball, Turner Hendricks, a colored Constable, was directed to convey him to Marlon, the county-seat, and lodge him in jail, pending his trial at the next term of the Circuit Court. White asked the Constable to accompany him to certain parties who, he affirmed, would give ball for his appearance; and also to go with him, in any event, to his cabin and permit him to bid his wife and children good-by. The officer refused, and, calling a man by the name of Swepson to his assistance, the three started for the little village, some distance away. Along the road Hendricks told all he met that he was "taking the desperado White to fall," and boasted of it as a remarkable feat. The prisoner said nothing, riding silently between his guards. Presently the Constable told him to ride up. As he spoke the desperado snatched a pistol from his bosom and discharged it at Hendricks, who fell from his horse on the ground, screaming that he was killed.

A STRANGE SCENE.

Quick as a flash both White and the other guard leaped from their horses, with drawn pistols. The desperado began to retreat, walking rapidly backward, but keeping his eyes on Swepson, and his pistol, a six-shooter, raised in readiness for immediate use. The thought of his prize escaping him roused Hendricks, who was not seriously wounded, and he got up and hurried after the desperado. The latter now left the road, and was crossing a fence when the Constable fired, the ball cutting a hole in the cont White wore. This made him furious. He turned and ran toward his pursuers, swearing he would cut their hearts from their bodies. For a moment the officer and guard were paralyzed at the sudden turn of affairs, but they quickly realized the situation. Hendricks fled as if pursued by demons, throwing away his pistols and everything that impeded his flight. The desperado sent a bullet flying after him, which took effect in his body, inflicting a wound from which he afterward died; and he then turned his attention to Swenson, whom he disarmed, and mounting his horse, rode away with a yell of triumph.

THE MURDER OF SHERIFF BEATTIE.

The news of White's daring escape, and the death of Constable Hendricks, spread through the county, creating tremendous excitement. Early the following morning Sheriff Beattie, with a posse, surrounded the cabin White occupied,—having learned that he had not attempted as yet to leave the country. White was at that moment making ready for his departure. His wife warned him of the approach of the posse. He sprang behind the bed at the moment the Sheriff pushed open the door and entered the cabin. As he crossed the threshold he caught sight of White, and leveled his gun at him, but the weapon missed fire. Before he could again pull the trigger, the desperado sent a bullet crashing through his head. Every precaution was taken to prevent the murderer's escape. A reward of several hundred dollars was offered for his capture. Printed descriptions of him were widely circulated.
