Hanged for Murder. MEMPHIS, TENN., June 10. — Hayes White, who murdered Sheriff W. F. Beattie, in Crittenden County, Arkansas, on April 21, was hanged at Marion this afternoon at two o'clock in the presence of 2,000 persons, 1,500 of whom were colored. The condemned man made a speech from the gallows, confessing the killing, but denying any knowledge that it was Sheriff Beattie whom he shot until he afterward saw him lying dead. It will be remembered that Sheriff Beattie was trying to effect the arrest of White, who was charged with burglary and made his escape from the colored constable who was taking him to jail three days previous. Sheriff Beattie was shot down by White as he entered the cabin at daylight on the date mentioned. A colored minister prayed with the condemned man on the gallows. White then sang a hymn, which was joined in by the colored people present. The black cap was arranged by the sheriff, who asked White if he was ready, to which he replied: "Yes; good-bye to all." The rope was cut and White was launched into eternity. The fall, although six feet, did not break his neck, and he died of strangulation. The body, after hanging eighteen minutes, was cut down and delivered to his friends for burial. The Arkansas Ku-Klux.

LITTLE Rock, ARK., June 10.—The county assessor and two other citizens of Perry County reached this city at noon to-day, claiming they had been compelled to flee for their lives. They were captured yesterday and roughly handled by their captors, who threatened to hang them this morning. They managed last night to elude the vigilance of their guards, and reached this city to-day in a decorable condition. Their feet were bleeding and torn, having walked the entire distance bare-footed. Great indignation exists among the law-abiding portion of the community. Governor Churchill will adopt summary measures to put down the outlaws.

Mrs. Hayes' Testimonial.

Mrs. Hayes' Testimonial.

CHICAGO, June 10.—The autograph testimonial album to Mrs. Rutherford B. Hayes by the women of Illinois has been finished. The work consists of six large volumes, 650 pages each, elegantly bound in full Turkey morocco. All through the volumes are scattered India ink drawings. The inscription reads: "From the ladies of Illinois who have admired the courage Mrs. Hayes has displayed in the administration of the hospitalities of the Executive Mansion. God grant that the influence of this signal and benign example may be felt more and more as age follows age in the life of this great Republic." The first signature is that of Mrs. James K. Polk, Nashville, Tenn.; the second that of R. B. Hayes. Among the autographs in volume 1 are those of members of the late Hayes Cabinet, Chief-Justice Waite and Justices of the Supreme Court, and Governors of nearly all the States and Territories, under the official seal, followed by Congressmen and prominent professional and business men.

LONDON, June 11.—The Standard's Dublin correspondent telegraphs as follows: Pressure is being brought to bear on the Irish executive to suppress the Land League by an order in council. The question is being gravely considered, owing to the representations made to the authorities by magistrates, county inspectors and others. I understand the law advisor and other Crown lawyers think the league is clearly an illegal organization, but the attorney-general strenuously holds out against assuming the responsibility for its suppression. A Heroic Dog.

Special Dispatch to The Bee

CHICAGO, January 6—10 p. m.—A fire occurred at 4 o'clock this morning in St. Lary's block, 42 and 44 Madison street. The only occupants were T. E. Lincoln, manufacturer of boots and shoes, his wife, and their faithful dog Jack. The dog discovered the fire, broke his chain and running to the door where Mr. and Mrs. Lincoln were asleep, yelped and howled furiously, finally bursting the door open. Mr. Lincoln was awakened by the animal licking his hand. The room was full of smoke, and escape by the stairs was cut off. Opening the window, Mr. Lincoln saw the firemen below, and threw to them his pocket-book, containing $193, with business papers and insurance. He then placed his wife outside on the ledge, and climbed out himself, hanging on to a swinging sign. Fully twenty minutes before the firemen got ladders up to rescue them the whole window saff fall upon him, cutting his hands and face. Both Mr. and Mrs. Lincoln were badly scorched by the flames shooting out at the window. The dog was also saved, but badly burned. Mr. Lincoln's loss is $10,000.

Many merchants here were connected with him in a business way, besides having money in his hands for investment. The greatest uneasiness exists, and nothing else is talked of on the streets.

Death's Ripe Harvest.

Special dispatch to The Bee.

CHICAGO, January 6—1 a. m.—The number of accidents and fatalities in Chicago yesterday was something extraordinary. In the first place there was the East Madison street fire, at 4 a. m., loss about $35,000, from which Mr. and Mrs. Lincoln barely escaped being badly burned and lacerated. Then came the State street fire, in running to which John Hawley, fireman, lost his life. An unknown man about 40 years old was killed on the Michigan Central road, at Kensington; another unidentified man hung himself in a shed on Washington street; Peter Callahan fell on the sidewalk and received injuries from which he died; Patrick Ross, shot in Sunday's row, died in the morning; Olif Carlson was struck by a Michigan Southern train and reported killed, but afterwards proved only three ribs broken; Mrs. Joanna Ryan dropped dead of fatty degeneration of the heart; Mrs. Agnetta Benson, while pursuing household duties, fell dead of heart disease, and to complete the list, Mrs. Mullen, in preparing a foot bath for her husband, let the babe fall from her arms into the water, and it was fatally scalded. Waltor H. Foster, an employee of The Times, and one of the oldest printers in Chicago, having come here with Mr. Storey from Michigan, died Tuesday of consumption, and was buried yesterday.

Special Dispatch to The Bee.

AUGUSTA, Me., January 6—1 a. m.—Mr. Hale's friends claim a majority of ten votes for United States senator, but if there is a change of six in this calculation, Mr. Hale cannot be nominated on the first ballot. Mr. Frye's supporters do not claim a majority, but assert that an allowance of fifteen should be made in Mr. Hale's count, and that they have a fair show for a majority on some of the latter ballots. They will stave off the proposition until next week, if possible. Mr. Hale is superintending his canvass in person, with Mr. S. S. Marble as chief of staff. Mr. Frye is represented by Judge Wing, of Auburn, and J. W. Weekfield, of Bath.

The Mechanies and Traders bank of Chattanooga has gone into liquidation. A national bank will doubtless be organized there in less than three months.

A Lawrence county man, seventy years of age, is in jail in Pulaski on the charge of manufacturing and uttering counterfeit money. Twenty years ago he served a term in the penitentiary for a similar crime.

The discussion of the comparative merits of the Grundy county and Rugby colonies continue to engross the attention of the papers in the eastern end of the State.

CRIMES AND CASUALTIES.
Two Men Hanged in Philadelphia.
PHILADELPHIA, JANUARY 24, PATRICK HAYES
CRIMES AND CASUALTIES.

Two Men Hanged in Philadelphia.
PHILADELPHIA, January 6 — Patrick Hayes and Daniel F. Sullivan paid the extreme penalty of the law in Moyamensing jail today. Hayes's crime was the murder of his wife, Bridget T. Hayes, whom he killed on the morning of March 23rd last. The couple had numerous quarrels and disputes over the property of Mrs. Hayes's children by her first husband, and had separated three weeks before the woman's murder. On the morning of the fatal day the man bought a pistol, had it loaded, and went to his wife's home, where he found her standing at the wash-tub. He immediately shot her twice, and then attempted suicide by shooting himself. Recovering from his self-inflicted injuries, Hayes was placed on trial in the Oyer and Terminer Court on June 21st last. Up to the day of the trial the prisoner had stoutly asserted that his wife had shot him and then shot herself, but in court he admitted his guilt, but contended that for an instant his mind was unbalanced, and in that moment the deed was committed.

The crime for which Sullivan was executed was the murder of Josephine S. Irwin, his paramour, on May 5, 1879, in a lodging-house on south Eighth street. Two years previous to her death Josephine separated from her husband, John Stanford, of Oil City, Pa., and came to this city to live with Sullivan, who was an agent for a minstrel troupe. Frequent quarrels took place between Sullivan and his mistress, the former accusing her of infidelity. Late on the night of the murder Sullivan returned home and immediately retired to his room, where his mistress was asleep. He there renewed his charges of infidelity. Shortly afterwards the report of a pistol was heard, and Sullivan called to the servant for assistance, saying Josephine had spot herself. The girl went to the room and found the woman in a dying condition, but able to charge Sullivan with having shot her, and he was arrested, and after the inquest committed for trial. The trial took place during the summer of 1879, and resulted in a verdict of murder in the first degree.

Execution in New Jersey.

NEWARK, N. J., January 6 — Mrs. Meierhoeffer, convicted with Frank Lammens, her paramour, of the murder of her husband, John Meierhoeffer, at West Orange, October 18, 1879, was hanged at the county court-house at 10½ o'clock this morning. She was very pale and deeply affected, but walked to the gallows without assistance, and met her fate without confessing or uttering a word. She died in about nine minutes, her neck being apparently unbroken. About thirty persons were present, including the officers and jury selected by the court under the recent law, and all spectators were excluded. Lammens was hanged from the same gallows immediately afterwards, but made no confession.

Missing light-House-Keepers.

NEW ORLEANS, January 6. — Seth W. Kipp, keeper of the Southwest Pass light-house, and his brother, James Kipp, his assistant, left Pilot Town on the afternoon of the 3d instant in a small sail-boat to return to the light house. Soon after the wind blew a hurricane from the westward, demolishing boat-houses, &c. Nothing has since been heard of the men or the boat, though search has been made in every direction. The United States light-house tender Pansy has been ordered to cruise in search of the missing men.
Murder in a Texas Bar-Room.
GALVESTON, January 6 — A special from Henrietta says that a man named Dan Rice having refused to drink with James Curtis an altercation arose, resulting in an exchange of shots. Curtis fell and expired within ten minutes. Rice was carried badly wounded to the doctor's office for treatment. As he was placed in a chair a bail was fired through the window, inflicting a mortal wound.

The Wintz Contempt Case.
NEW ORLEANS, January 6. — President Wintz, of the New Orleans City Railroad Company, having been released from the parish prison in the contempt case, was again before the grand jury yesterday, and underwent a lengthy examination concerning an alleged bribery of city officials in a matter of securing franchise for his company. Wintz was finally discharged by the grand jury, which is an indication that he answered all important questions.

A Wheeling (W Va.) Official Discharged from Custody.
WHEELING, W. Va., January 6. — The case of the State against John L. Maxwell, charged with embezzling funds of the City Gas Office, and which has been on trial for six days, abruptly terminated yesterday by the discharge of the prisoner on technical grounds raised by his counsel that he was not an officer of the city, as charged in the indictment.

Died from the Effects of a Stab.
DANVILLE, Va., January 6. — Last night Ben. Lampkin (colored) died from the effects of a stab received by him the night previous while attempting to arrest a chicken-thief in the hen-house of Councilman Allen (colored). The chicken-thief escaped and has not been apprehended. He is unknown.

Wouldn't Be Whipped.

NEW YORK, January 6 — A special from Murfreesboro', Tenn., says a band of masked men called on Henry Miller (colored) to whip him for alleged arson. He refused to come out, and, firing a shot gun, he killed one of the party, L. B. Newman. The mob fled.

When last heard from the murderers had not been arrested, and the Marshal had taken no steps looking that way. AN OBLIVIOUS MAN. The Strange Adventures of a Latch-Key And the Tale It Doth Unfold.
A few nights ago a young man who lives not a hundred miles from Second and Madison streets, came home in a very absent-minded manner. It was a trifle late, and this fact made him probably still more oblivious of passing events. He placed his key in the door and went on up-stairs, leaving the key on the outside in the lock. His room-mate comes in by the back door, and, of course did not see the key. The next night the absent-minded man came home again late, felt in his pocket and could find no key. He began pounding at the door and brought down his room-mate in his baseball suit. The following dialogue ensued:

"Who's there?"
"Me."
"Where's your key?"
"I have lost it."

The man on the inside pulled at the door and it opened. The key was still in the lock. He took it out, handed it to his friend and said with commiseration:

"How did you come so. I am sincerely sorry for you."

"What do you mean?"
"That's all right, my boy; come up-stairs."

"OLD-TIME NIGGER DOGS"

To be Placed on Guard Over a Gentleman's Chicken Ranch.

Yesterday afternoon several gentlemen were congregated in the office of Mr. Charles L. Pullen, Secretary of the Legislative Council, when that gentleman announced that he was negotiating for a "nigger dog." Mr. Pullen is a well-known poultry fancier, and has some very fine game stock which possesses a great fascination for the sneak thief. In order to secure the safety of his fowls and to detect, if necessary, a thief, he has purchased a "nigger dog." The subject of the "nigger dog" was then taken up by those present, and one gentleman described some of the feats and peculiarities of the animal. "What kind of a dog is a "nigger dog?" asked the APPEAL reporter.

"It's a regular bloodhound. It was employed before the war to find stray negroes." "Does it always spot its man?" "Yes, sir; it can keep one track in a hundred. Even when a man swims a stream it can follow him. I have seen it put on a trail that had been plowed up and follow it as unerringly as if it were an open one."

"Is there no way to baffle the animal?" "Yes, there is one. If you sprinkle a little blood on the trail it will break the dog all up, so to speak. You can hear him yelp for a mile, almost, when he comes to it."

"They were used in slave times?" "Yes; there were a number of men who had packs of them, and they made considerable money out of them. For instance a slave owner lost a negro. He went to the party owning the dogs and offered him fifty or a hundred dollars to bring back the runaway. They were not used to tear the negroes to pieces, but merely as detectives. They were held in by long slender chains, and they could always scent a man thirty or forty yards, and they would always bark furiously when they discovered the object of their search."

"Are there many of them now?" "No, sir; they are almost entirely thinned out. The negroes hate them as you would a snake, and never lose an opportunity to poison them."

"Are they in use now?" "Yes, the boss of a gang of convicts has had several, but most of them have been poisoned by the negroes. He has now only two."

"Have you ever followed one of them on the chase?" "Yes; in 1876 I was living in Mississippi. In our neighborhood, a negro caught a white man in the woods and tried to cut his throat with a penknife. Some white men coming up were just in time to see the darky running away. He was too fleet for them and they had to give up the chase. There were several
with a penknife. Some white men coming up were just in time to see the darky running away. He was too fleet for them and they had to give up the chase. There were several of us, however, who got an old "nigger dog" and started at three o'clock in the afternoon after the criminal. It was the rarest sport I ever had. I tell you it was exciting. We rode on over hills, through woods until it was sundown and we had not yet bagged our man. We were in for it, however, and kept it up in the dark. The excitement then increased. We dashed away past dark, gloomy forests in silence with the fearful yelp of the dog only to break it. About midnight we came upon our man, whom we secured and took home. We rode twenty-three miles after him and the dog never faltered for an instant. These "nigger dogs" seem to be able to run forever. They never tire out until they have caught their man."

This is the kind of animal Mr. Pullen proposes to have in his chicken ranch. As the gentleman described the terrible attributes of the "nigger dog," the genial Secretary was regarded with eyes of dilated horror, and the reporter, shading his eyes, fled from the room.

The body of Miss Watson was found in the woods Saturday after she had been missing four days." GUITEAU IN NEW YORK Twelve Years Ago, and the Miserable Part He Played.
NEW YORK, July 4. About twelve years ago, when the Essex Market Police Court had become notorious as a place where all sorts of crimes could be compromised by venal Police Justices, a number of shysters, broken down lawyers and practitioners, ruined by liquors were to be met with daily at that Court. These misnamed lawyers would often hunt up cases for the Police Justice, and share in the spoils, and on one occasion a fight occurred in Court between a magistrate and a shyster upon the division of half a dollar. Among these shysters was Charles Guiteau, who had part of an office in rear of a liquor store on the southeast corner of Broome and Essex streets. Guiteau's merit consisted mainly in the nefarious manner in which he would secure cases, and many an innocent person would be mulled in the shape of a fine for an offense he had never committed, while thieves, vile women and such offenders against the law would be allowed to escape if they had only enough money to compromise the case. One of Guiteau's practices was to cause the arrest of the Bowyer demi-mondes who had not previously paid him a fee; have women locked up at night, and appear for them next morning as a lawyer at the Essex Market Court, and thus share the fine which was certain to be imposed.

8. Kurino, a Japanese student, writes to the Boston Herald that his love of his own country impels him to set forth "a nationality utterly distinct from that of China." The principal reasons given by him for rejecting the theory that the Japanese are of Chinese origin are that the customs of the two people are generally different; that the former are far superior to the

CASUALTIES.

DROWNED.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
LA Crosse, Wis., July 5.—Late yesterday afternoon Joseph Heller, a German boy, was drowned in La Crosse River, near this city. Heller, together with other boys, went in the water for the purpose of bathing. He was a good swimmer. He was 15 years old and a printer by trade.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
Toledo, O., July 5.—The body of a stranger, supposed to have been that of J. Gill Gagem, of Lafayette, Ind., was pulled out of the river opposite the city this afternoon, where he had probably been drowned a day or two ago. His clothes were found on the shore yesterday. As they were somewhat bloody, the theory of foul play was at first entertained.

RUN OVER AND KILLED.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

EAST SAGINAW, Mich., July 5.—Andrew Quackenbush, a cooper by trade, was run over last night by an engine on the Jackson, Lausing & Saginaw Road, near Saginaw City, crushing his arms and legs and causing death. He was intoxicated at the time.

HANNIBAL, Mo., July 5.—Jerry Yancey, agent of the Keokuk Packet Company for many years, and W. J. Connor, of De Soto, Mo., were run over and killed by the cars about noon to-day. Yancey was well known all along the river.

A RUNAWAY TEAM.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

URBANA, Ind., July 5.—This afternoon, while out driving, Mrs. Andrew Freeshout's team became unmanageable and ran away, throwing her from the buggy, and probably inflicted fatal injuries. Her cousin, Mrs. Corn Freeshout, who was with her, was seriously injured.

KILLED BY A HORSE.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

PAXTON, Ill., July 5.—While leading a horse to water yesterday, having tied the rope around his wrist, a little son of John B. Johnson, living south of Elliott, this county, was thrown down and dragged over the ground until dead.

POISONED AT A PICNIC.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

KANSAS CITY, Mo., July 5.—The reported poisoning at Harrisonville picnic July 4 was greatly exaggerated. No one is dead, and only five or six persons were made sick by drinking lemonade, none seriously.

THROWN FROM A HORSE.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

DUNQUE, In. July 5.—W. Griffin, a young man, of Prairie Creek Township, was thrown from a horse to-day, and his life is despaired of.

RUN OVER BY AN ENGINE.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
WATERTOWN, WIs., July 5.—Thomas McCann, a brakeman on the Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railway, was run over here to-day by an engine and had his left foot cut off.

OBITUARY.

William Inman, Steamship Owner.

A cable dispatch announces the death of William Inman, the founder of the Inman line of steamships trading between Liverpool and New York. He was a native of Liverpool, and, after receiving a liberal education, entered into mercantile life. In the year 1859 he was a junior partner in the firm of Messrs. Richardson Brothers & Co., shipowners, and agents for the Liverpool, New York & Philadelphia Steamship Company, which was formed early in that year. Mr. Inman was appointed to manage the shipping department of the business. He it was who inaugurated the idea of affording to the poorer classes of emigrants comfortable voyages in steamships to the United States, and at a rate within their means. The experiment succeeded, and the horrors of the passage in old packet ships soon became a thing of the past, the sailing vessels once confined to this branch of the carrying business being driven out of the trade. At that time the Atlantic steamers were by no means the perfection of naval architecture that they are now. The vessels of the Cunard, Collins, and Vanderbilt Lines were propelled by sidewheels, and the screw, as a means of propulsion across the Atlantic had scarcely been dreamed of. Mr. Inman, however, was of the opinion that the screw was destined to be the motive power of the steamships of the future, and at his instance the City of Glasgow, owned by the Liverpool, New York, and Philadelphia Line was dispatched on her first voyage, screw propelled, in mid-winter. So great was the alarm in shipping circles as to the danger of the experiment that underwriters charged a special rate of insurance. Mr. Inman's prognostications turned out to be correct. The City of Glasgow made her voyages with speed and safety, and she was in truth the pioneer of the magnificent steamships which now ply across the Atlantic. Side-wheels were soon abandoned by the regular lines and scow propellers were adopted. New York had in 1850 become the port of the Cunard Line. The City of Glasgow and the City of Manchester were sent to Philadelphia, and it was not till 1857 that the Inman steamers came to New York. In October, 1854, Mr. Inman became sole managing partner of the Company, which assumed his name, the firm of Richardson Brothers retiring from the agency. That position he filled until the present time with eminent success. He first inaugurated the system of touching at Queenstown in connection with the North Atlantic trade, and the City of Baltimore was the first to commence the regular calling in 1857. All the other lines in time followed Mr. Inman's lead. He was also first to adopt the lane routes across the North Atlantic recommended by Lieut. Maury, of the United States Navy, thereby decreasing the dangers of the voyage by collision with ice. Another of the mechanical changes brought about by Mr. Inman is worthy of record. It was the superseding of the old plain engine by the new compound type. BRIEF TELEGRAMS.
City of Mexico: The attempted assassination of Garfield has caused great indignation here.

Long Branch: Heat terrible; 98 to 101°. Grant just received a most encouraging dispatch about the president.

New York: Both the Times and Tribune have stinging leaders on the duty of the New York legislature in the present crisis.

Ryersford: Fire destroyed the stove works of Kelly, Springs & Co. Loss $100,000; fully insured. Several persons were injured.

Cincinnati: Unolula won the 2:20 race; best time 2:27. Fannie Cook won the mile dash; time 1:44¾. The pacing race was a walk over.

Jackson, N. Y.: A tenement house at Duke village was burned. Three children named Moody, (colored), aged four, six and ten years perished.

New Albany, Ind.: Wm. Willis and Robert Prunett, living near here, settled a feud by a duel. Willis was dangerously wounded. Prunett unhurt.

Springfield, Mass. Blackington & Co's. woolen mills, at Maple Grove, Adams, Mass., are burned. Loss $100,000; about $50,000 insurance. Loss of stock to Colory Bros. & Co., who ran the mill, $20,000; half insured; 125 employees.

New York: Representatives of the grand army of the republic and veteran soldiers and sailors, met to-night and heard addresses and adopted resolutions on the assassination. A letter from Gen. Isaac Catlin, disapproving of the meeting, caused a storm of hisses.

Cincinnati: Evidences of crooked dealing on the part of Guitteau, while a Chicago lawyer, are turning np here. He got permission to settle a claim for one firm at 15 cents on the dollar; he settled it for 100 cents and never turned over a dollar to the creditors. He was debarred for this.

Washington: The story that the assassin Guitteau tried to shoot Blaine, but was prevented by Benson, formerly of the secret service, is disproved by the testimony of ticket agent Park, at the depot, who says Guitteau tried to escape as soon as the shooting was over. Benson was not in the room at the time
Monticello, Ark.: It is certain that Edmunds ruined Miss Sallie Watson and then murdered her. She disappeared while out with a party of men, and was never seen alive again. Her body has been found, with the head cut entirely off with an axe, and Edmunds has been arrested from indubitable evidence. Lynching is feared.

howel-edmuns-monticello-1881-07-11.A10:
A Double Crime for Which the Law Does Not Provide Anything Like Adequate Punishment. Details of the Murder of Miss Sallie Watson, of Drew County, Ark., by H. G. Edmunds.
From Mr. Terrell Harris, who came up from Monticello yesterday, we learn the following particulars of the horrible murder of the daughter of Mr. James R. Watson, which was committed on last Thursday morning: The young lady, Miss Sallie Watson, was about seventeen years of age and very attractive. She was seen at the cow-pen on her father's premises talking with her brother-in-law, H. G. Edmunds. From the cow-pen she went to the house, and leaving the milk unstrained, she put on a clean dress and left. This was the last time she was seen alive. Upon missing her, search was at once instituted by the family, who could find no trace of the missing one. On the morning the unfortunate young lady was missed, Mr. Stephen Gaster (another brother-in-law) and H. G. Edmunds went fishing on the Saline river. The parents of the missing girl, thinking that she had gone fishing with them, started a courier down the river to see if such was the fact. When the courier arrived at the river and found the parties, he told them of the missing girl. Edmunds, who was in a boat with Mr. Gaster, seemed to be very much excited, and when asked what was the matter with him said that he had a chill. The two parties went home immediately, and the search for the missing girl was continued. Edmunds said perhaps the girl had ran away and married. Acting on his own suggestion, he started for Monticello to look over the marriage register. While in Monticello, it is said that he acted very strangely, and that he drank about a quart of whisky, which seemed to have no effect upon him. In the meantime the search was continued but without avail, until the arrival of Dr. Kersh and wife, who had been sent for by the troubled family. The attention of Dr. Kersh was attracted by an offensive smell as he drew near the premises of Mr. Watson, and on arriving at the house he proposed to go in the direction where he first noticed the same, to search for the girl. Edmunds objected strongly to going in the direction indicated by Dr. Kersh and said the girl must surely have gone in another direction. Dr. Kersh insisted on going in the way that he proposed, and accordingly started out, followed by the family and a few others. About two or three hundred yards from the house a buzzard was seen to fly upward, and on going to the place the body of the murdered girl was found. She was lying upon the ground covered with a few bushes. There were several gashes in her head that had been made with a sharp instrument. Facts then began to accumulate. A little daughter of Mr. Watson's had seen Edmunds talking with her sister at the cowpen, and heard him invite her sister to meet him soon thereafter. A negro woman saw him pass her cabin Thursday morning with a shot-gun and a hand-ax. The ax was found. There was blood on its handle. The gaps in the ax corresponded with places made thereby in the head of the murdered girl, and with places made on the bushes that were cut down to cover the body with. These facts, taken together with Edmunds's strange behavior, and other circumstances which need not be mentioned here, led to his arrest. The body of the unfortunate girl had lain in the bushes from Thursday morning until Saturday evening. Edmunds was arrested by Mr. Stephen Gaster and carried to Monticello, where he was lodged in jail. An attempted seduction is thought to be the cause of this terrible tragedy. The fiend in human shape who committed this horrible crime was a nephew as well as son-in-law of Mr. Watson, having married Miss Minnie Stitt. We learn that excitement is running very high, and it is thought that the villain will be lynched by the infuriated citizens. Mr. Watson is well-known in Pine Bluff, and has many friends here who deeply deplore this great trouble that has overtaken his family. Since the foregoing was in type we learn that Edmunds's wife contended for his innocence until yesterday, when she found his bloody shirt. She then sent him word that she was satisfied of his guilt, and would have nothing further to do with him. It will be remembered that the murdered girl was Mrs. Edmunds's sister.

FIVE inmates of the reform school at Portland, Me., threw pepper in the eyes of Keeper Flint, knocked him down, took his keys, and escaped.

DEUTLER, the Chicagoan who killed his wife on Sunday evening, shot himself dead at the corner of Fullerton und Western avenues, where he was found with the pistol beside him.

JOSKPH MANN, a conductor on the Lackawanna road, was killed near Portland, Pa., by his brother-in-law, Stewart Garrison, a former brakeman, in revenge for being discharged.

MARGARET WILSON, a muscular Irishwoman of New York, dragged Francis Farrell into an alley near Fifty-ninth street, and struck him with a saucepan, when her husband robbed the victim of his week's wages.

ISAIAH NOBLE, a farmer living near New Holland.
Isaiah Noble, a farmer living near New Holland, O., accidentally ran a reaper over his little four-year-old boy, crushing his head and instantly killing him. The child was lying asleep in the track of the machine.

Miss Sallie Watson, aged 16, the beautiful daughter of J. R. Watson, a wealthy citizen of Drew County, Ark., was lately missed from her home near Monticello, and after a brief search her dead and mutilated body was found in an adjacent woods. Howell Edmunds, brother-in-law of the deceased, who has heretofore borne a good name, was arrested on the charge of committing the murder, and so strong were the proofs against him that he narrowly escaped lynching.

"Doc." Thomas and his brother, Marion Thomas, have been arrested, charged with the robbery of the stage between Seligman and Eureka Springs, Ark., on the night of March 10.

Further information concerning the recent massacre of a party of Americans in Mexico by Indians is to the effect that the victims were not railroad engineers, as at first supposed, but a party of travelers going by coach to Chihuahua. The Indians ambushed the coach and fired upon it, killing the driver at once and the two lead mules. The passengers, seven in number, were then taken out and five of them killed, viz: Charles Greene, of Independence, Kans.; Larie Fordham, of Boston, Mass.; Guy Levitt, of Indiana; George Wallace, of Taylorville, Ill., and Charles Haines, of Kansas. Greene's body was burned. The other bodies were all scorched. Thomas R. Pugh, one of the passengers, and son of ex-Senator Pugh, was taken prisoner by the Indians. What his fate is has not yet been learned. The other passenger, Thomas Cummerford, of San Francisco, Cal., and the conductor escaped in the darkness. The Indians were a remnant of Victorio's Apaches. The Mexican authorities have already dispatched several bodies of troops to the Cancelario Mountains to scout for these Indians, and Gov. Terrasas will order Mexican Federal troops from Chihuahua to scout the stage road, and will also furnish an escort for stage coaches.

Two children of Samuel Grippen, at West Troy, N. Y., were suffocated by the burning of some fire-crackers stored in the room where they were sleeping.

SOLOMON MERRICK, James H. White and James Alexander Bartum, the latter colored, were killed outright; James Cox, colored, mortally scalded; Edward Sheehan badly, though not dangerously scalded, and four other hands badly injured by the explosion of a portable engine on the farm of Edward Sheehan, in Talbott County, Md., on the 6th.

FRED HYLAND and Mark Folsom, both about 12 years of age, were drowned in Coon Creek, near Des Moines, Iowa, on the 7th.

A DAUGHTER of Major-General Fyres, of England, recently fell overboard at Hyenes, France. Her mother and two sisters sought to rescue her, and all four were drowned.

POSTMASTER C. E. Carman, at Lyons, Mich., accidentally shot and killed his 14-year-old son the other night. The boy had wandered out on the roof in a fit of somnambulism and his father mistook him for a burglar.

THE LAPRADE MURDERERS In Danger from the Excited Citizens of Springfield, in this State—Militia Asked For. Governor Hawkins Dispatches Fifty Men to the Scene—A Sheriff's Posse to Act in the Interim.
NASHVILLE, February 14.—The murder of Laprade was one of the most diabolical crimes on record. Nine negroes banded together to rob Laprade, who was supposed to have fallen heir to a large amount of money. On getting into his house, by imitating his brother's voice, they bore him to the floor and demanded his money, when he gave up five dollars, all he had. Thinking to extort from him the whereabouts of his money, they singed the hair from his head and body, tore the tendons from his legs, hanged him repeatedly, dragged him about the yard and crushed his skull with an ax. A confession of the crime was extorted from an old negro named Jim Higgins by roasting his feet. On the night of the 15th of September, 1880, Bell and Jamison, two negroes who led in the murder of Laprade, were lynched, and a white man named Jamison, who had shot a young lady because she had declined his attentions was shot to death in his cell, after a most desperate encounter. Higgius was brought to Nashville with those sent to Springfield. To-day he had to have one of his feet amputated, and died in jail. A special dispatch says a mob of forty persons came to Springfield to-night, but were persuaded by the citizens to let the law take its course.

NASHVILLE, February 14.—Governor Hawkins received a dispatch from Judge Stark, at Springfield, this evening, asking him to send twenty-five to fifty men to protect the five negro murderers of Laprade, sent from Nashville this morning for trial, as they were to be mobbed to-night. The governor telegraphed to Stark he would send men as soon as possible, and ordered the sheriff of Robertson county to summon the whole force of the county to protect the prisoners. NASHVILLE. February 17.—To-day was the most uneventful one of the session.

In the senate a resolution making coupons not receivable for taxes was tabled—14 to 10.

The LaPrade Murderers.

Special to the Appeal.

SPRINGFIELD, TENN., February 17.—The evidence in the case of the LaPrade murderers closed this afternoon with the testimony of fifteen witnesses for the defense. Bill Murphy, one of the gang, was to have been brought on the stand. THE OBJECT OF THEIR VISIT.

NASHVILLE, February 17.—The object of the military being sent to Winchester to tomorrow morning is to bring the Poe murderers to the Nashville jail after their preliminary trial.

Bound to See the Show.

NASHVILLE, February 17.—An invitation to the legislature to be present at the inauguration of Garfield was adopted by that body, and nearly every member will leave here on the night of March 2d for Washington.

Troops Ordered to Winchester.

NASHVILLE, February 17.—The governor has received a telegram from Judge Williams, at Winchester, saying: "The preliminary examination of the two negroes for the murder of Baker will be held to-morrow morning. If the charge is proven, which is thought probable, they will be lynched. The sheriff at this time is absent summoning witnesses. Send him at least forty men to-night. SNOWED UNDER AGAIN.

Chicago Smothered Beneath a Five-Inch Fall of Snow.

CHICAGO, February 17.—Since 8 o'clock this evening nearly five inches of snow has fallen, and it is still coming down at the rate of an inch or two an hour. It is very compact, and lies where it falls, and will prove a great hindrance to railroad and foot travel. Coming as it does upon the heavy snows which have covered the ground almost without interruption since the middle of last November, this heavy fall of snow is quite remarkable and noteworthy. The air is cold and rawish, with no signs of a thaw.

THE OLD DOMINION.

Through the Democracy, Makes an Appeal for Homest Government.

RICHMOND, February 17.—The Conservative Democratic State central committee have called a convention at this city for August 4th next. An address has been is used giving a brief history of the organization of the party. It says: "What Republican triumph in southern commonwealths means let the wretched record of fifteen years attest. It signifies, in a word, the dethronement of the virtue, character, intelligence and prosperity of the State and the erection on their ruins of a dynasty of profligacy, ignorance and malice, whose unvarying fruits in the southern States have been social degradation, universal robbery and continued disorders."

SEVEN NEGRNES LYNCHED.
FIVE HANGED ON THE FRONT OF A TENNESSEE COURT HOUSE AND TWO IN THE WOODS.
SPRINGFIELD, Tenn., Feb. 19.—The country is to-day in a fever-heat of excitement over the wholesale lynching which occurred last night. The tragedy which culminated last night in the lynching of the five negroes implicated in the murder of Mr. Laprade, makes a total of ten deaths which have thus far resulted from the fearful butchery. The crime for which these negroes were lynched was the murder of a farmer named Laprade, who lived alone near Sadlersville, Robinson county, about a mile away from any neighbor. The report was current that he and his two brothers had fallen heirs to $9,000 a few days before the murder. A party of nine negroes went to his house on the night of September 8, 1880. Going in the rear of his dwelling, one of them knocked at the door, and, imitating the voice of Laprade's brother, asking admission, Laprade opened the door without thought of harm. The nine negroes rushed in upon him, knocked him down and then demanded all his money. He gave them $5, saying that was all he had. Throwing a rope around his neck they dragged him about his grounds, hanged him to the limb of a tree repeatedly until he was almost unconscious, singed his body with torches and lacerated and multilated him with knives in the endeavor to compel him to admit that he had concealed the money, but always with the same result. With the rope he was dragged about the yard, and nameless outrages were committed upon his person. Finally, his legs were cut and hacked, and the tendons torn from their places from the knee down. Then his skull was crushed in with an axe, after which the body was hidden under some bushes in a neighboring thicket. The body was found two weeks afterwards.

The discovery of the murder caused intense excitement, and threats of lynching were freely made against the murderers as soon as they should be apprehended. Suspicion fell upon Jim Higgins, and after being imprisoned some days, he made a confession implicating his associates, who were arrested. Higgins who was an old negro, was taken out and his feet burned until, in his agony, he is said to have given the details of the Laprade murder. The prisoners, including Higgins, were brought to the Nashville jail. Higgins had one of his feet amputated and subsequently died in jail.

September 15 two of the murderers, Bell and Jameson, were taken from the Springfield jail and lynched. On the same night a white man named Ramsey was shot to death in his cell. He had been confined for shooting a Miss Holt, whom he began to persecute on account of her engagement with another person.

About 10.30 o'clock on the night of the 14th of the present month some twenty-five mounted men rode into town and proceeded to the jail. They intended to lynch the prisoners, but desisted on being informed that the trial would proceed, and if guilty the negroes would be hanged. The trial of the prisoners had been in progress all yesterday and in the evening it had reached a termination in the charge of Judge Stroke to the jury. The five murderers, James Elder, Loch Mallory, Lun Stell, Robert Thweat and another whose name has not been ascertained, were delivered to the custody of the Sheriff, and that official prepared to start to the jail with them. Bill Murphy and Anthony Duffy, who testified for the State, were set at liberty and it is thought that their release led to the terrible tragedy. As the Sheriff departed with his prisoners he was met at court-room door by an infuriated mob, who presenting pistols at his head, rushed upon him and took the trembling murderers from him. Attorney-General Bell tried to collect a posse to resist the mob, but failed, and was compelled to make his exit through a window.

The mob ordered all the lights out, fired a regular fusilade of shots to intimidate any would-be rescuers, dragged the five captives to the east door of the Court-House, where ropes were awaiting them. The ropes were suspended from the veranda above. The five bodies in an instant were swinging beneath the veranda. Jim Elder was the only one who made any struggle and he was quickly thrown down, bound hand and foot and then hanged with the others. The mob guarded the bodies until they were sure that their work was completed and life extinct. The leader then gave the order, "Disperse, my mem, to your homes," and the executioners—some 200 in number—immediately departed, going on horseback in three different directions. The crowd attending the trial was parlyzed with terror at first, and then jumped from the windows of the court-room and rushed off in every direction, uttering cries of affright. There was no whiskey in the crowd of lynchers, and they were under strict discipline. No outsiders were allowed to approach until all the negroes were pronounced dead and then it was announced that the man who would cut them down would do so at his peril.

This morning the two murderers, Duffy and Murphy, who turned State's evidence, were found hanging to a tree near the scene of the murder. This makes seven lives that were sacrificed by the lynchers last night.

Public sentiment sustains the action of the mob. The people feared an appeal would be made and a new trial granted the prisoners. The testimony was regarded as strong, proving the guilt of the murderers, and there was no fear that the jury would not convict them.

SAD FATE OF A FORMER HICKMAN
LADY.—Mrs. Atkinson, and infant child,
were found in the river, near her home,
at Stewart's Landing, with skull crushed,
and every evidence of having been violently dealt with. The New Madrid Record says, it was known that she had been in domestic trouble with her husband, James Adkinson, and a separation followed. They had two children, the husband kept one and she took the other and went to her father's, Mr. Batsell, who lives in the same neighborhood.

Last Sunday evening the wife took her child and went to her husband, hoping to bring about a reconciliation. Next morning the woman and her youngest child were missing, which caused considerable talk in the neighborhood and a search was instituted. Atkinson, who had been taking the matter very coolly, suddenly disappeared when the search commented. It was found that tracks of a woman's shoe led from the house to the river bank, a few yards distant, and a barefoot track could be traced back to the house. At the point where the shoe tracks reached the bank there were marks that something had been thrown into the water. It was remembered by the neighbors that Akinson had small feet and could wear his wife's shoes. Searching the house the wife's shoes were found concealed between the feather and straw beds.

Being satisfied that Atkinson had killed his wife on Sunday night, had worn her shoes while carrying her body to the river bank to conceal his crime, here took them off and carried them back to the house in his hand and concealed them between the beds, the horror-stricken relatives and friends proceeded to drag the river for the body. On Tuesday the body was recovered, which plainly showed that the woman had met a violent death. Her head was badly beaten by some blunt instrument and her neck showed that she had been choked. No shoes were on the body when recovered, and the theory is advanced that Atkinson wore her shoes while carrying the body to the bank to give color to a story that she committed suicide.
The body of the infant was also found in the river, near where the mother was found.
The Batsell family, years ago, lived in Hickman, and are well known to many of our people.

NEW MADRID, July 18.—It is reported that James Atkinson, the murderer of his wife and child, who has been in jail at Gayoso since his arrest July 10th, was taken from the jail last night and lynched. The murder of Mrs. Adkinson and child of which mention was made in last week. Courier, is still exciting our Missouri neighbors, and is involved in great mystery. The friends of Adkinson indicate that on the final trial his innocence of the dreadful crime of murdering his wife and own infant child will be made to appear. The Adkinson version of the affair is, that the father of Mrs. Adkinson, the murdered woman, had driven her from their home, and told her that she might find shelter elsewhere, and under these circumstances she went back to her husband from whom she had been separate. The husband refused her permission to come into his yard, but she continued to loiter about his premises until late in the night he invited her in and they patchd up some kind of a compromise of their domestic troubles, one condition of the compromise being that not one of her father's family were ever to come on his premises. The next morning the wife cooked breakfast and Adkinson went to work on the farm. Soon after breakfast, Mrs. Batsell, the mother of Mrs. Adkinson, feeling anxious to know the result of affairs, went over to Adkinson's and inquired of her daughter if a reconciliation had been fixed up. The daughter replied to her mother that they had "sorter made up." While this interview was progressing, Adkinson returned to the house, and ordered Mrs. Batzell to leave, and got his pistol and threatened to shoot the old lady if she did not leave. He succeeded in driving her off, and witnesses had to interfere to prevent his shooting her. The theory is that Mrs. Adkinson being driven to desperation by being driven from her own father's house, and her mother being driven from her husband's house, that she committed suicide, and killed her own child and herself. The little 5 year old girl states that the mother gave her and the little baby white powders and took some heres.

The bodies of Mrs. Adkinson and her infant child were found in the river near the husband's house. The tracks leading from the house to the river were small shoes exactly the size Mrs. Adkinson wore, and the tracks returning from the river to the house were barefooted. When Mrs. Adkinson's body was found in the river, she had on no shoes, and the only pair of shoes she owned was found in the house under the bed. If she wore them from the house to the river when she drowned herself, as the tracks indicated, how came her shoes back in the house?

Investigation proved that the husband wore exactly the same size, and had frequently worn his wife's shoes. In addition to this circumstantial evidence, the husband fled the neighborhood; but claims that he did so, because warned by his relatives to do so on the ground that the people would mob him before the real facts could be brought out. Report mays that the 5 year old child, who first sated that the mother had given her the white powder, being removed from the father, stated that her father had tied the baby and her mother together with a rope. Report, also, says, that old man Adkinson, on the morning of the unfortunate air, had made his threats that he intended to go over there and make his son kill his wife and throw her in the river; and that on the same morning he had told parties that his son's wife had poisoned himself, probably an hour before the killing; or

KINGTON INTELLIGENCER, SATURDAY, JULY 23, 1881.
The magnitude and rapid increase of the beer industry in this country is fully set forth in "Wing's Brewer's hand book" for 1881, published as an annual supplement to the Western Brewer. The advance-sheets of the fifth volume of the hand book, which is the official authority for the bewers and malsters in the United States and Canada, show that about two hundred new breweries were established during the year ending May 1, 1881, and that there were over five hundred changes in the business during the same time. While the sale of beer in the United States in 1877 was only 9,752,030 barrels, the total sales for the year ending May 1, 1881, amounted to 14,125,466 barrels, an increase of 4,373,436 barrels in five years, or an average annual increase of about 1,000,060 barrels, and an increase over 1880 of 1,324,566 barrels.

Some not overly reputable newspapers in St. Louis, where they seem to have lost the art of properly condemning murderers to the gallows, have been denouncing Judge Sherwood, of the supreme court, for exercising his legal duty in seeing that Kring, a woman killer, has a proper hearing of some sort of an appeal. The lawyers down there are considerably muddled about the matter; it is only those who know no law that seem to clearly assert that Judge Sherwood doesn't know his business. A gambler might safely lay 10 to 1 on the proposition that his critics know theirs less thoroughly.

After Aug. 1 the cable companies announce that the rate per word to the United States and Canada will be one shilling, one-half the present price. Press rates continue the same as heretofore. It is thought by many that the prices will be further reduced after Gould's cable gets in operation. It is the opinion of experts that the companies, if properly managed, could afford to forward press matter for three cents a word.

The business of the New York stock exchange has almost quadrupled during the past year and a half. The exchange now has members through the United States, including nearly all the principal cities of the Union. The membership is limited to 1,100, and not likely to be increased. A seat which could have been bought a few years ago for 5,000 is now worth $30,000. It is expected the price will yet reach 50,000.

N. Y. Tribune:—"When he is fairly out of the way it will be natural for the newspapers to speak kindly of the late primate. First and last he was a most fruntful tropic, whatever else he was. We shall never look upon his like again for a long time." No; that you won't. You'll know the force of never looking on his like again in the next election.

"These greenback fellows," says the Detroit Post, "are only imitators of the rebel secretary of the treasury, as the facetious scoundrels making war on the government used to call Meminger." The idiot who denominates southern soldiers "scoundrels" no doubt considers himself a patriot and a gentleman. The chances are that he is neither.

Representative Chalmers, of Mississippi, who has published a card against Senator Lemar, is it so cold, ambitious to occupy that gentleman's place in the senate. Mr. Chalmers seems to have an attack of Conklemaula. It he don't recover sooner the democratic legislature will cure him of it when it meets.

A disgraceful scene of disorder took place in the New York legislature, Monday. The second joint ballot was conducted amid the greatest confusion, the members standing and hooting each one as his name was called, and firing paper balls at each other. Speaker Sharpe was paired with a stalwart.

James Atkinson, who has been in jail at Gayoso, Mo., since his arrest, July 10th, was, it is reported, taken from jail Monday night and lynched. He was charged with murdering his wife and child, July 4th, and throwing their bodies into the river, where they were found.

Joseph A. Kline, a young man found guilty last week of murder in the second degree for poisoning his father last fall, was sentenced at Canton, Ohio, July 15, by Judge Meyer, to imprisonment for life in the penitentiary, six months of each of the first five years to be passed in solitary confinement.

Hillsboro, Mo., Democrat:—"Republicans have long amused themselves by referring to the democratic party as a party of hungry office seekers, and yet no democrat ever got office-hungry enough to shoot the president because his demands were not complied with."

Speaker Sharpe, of the New York general assembly, deserted the Conkling phalanx a few days ago, explaining that he had had a revelation that the majority should rule. Naughty Sharp! he knew that all the time; his revelation came from Jimmy G.

Charles Atkins was arrested at Goshen, Ill., July 15, upon a requisition from Gov. Foster, of Ohio, upon the charge of horse-stealing. It is alleged he stole eight horses at Bryan, Ohio, and a few from other places. He was taken back to that place.

A terrible cyclone swept over the village of New Ulm, Minnesota, Friday afternoon of last week. Fourteen persons were killed; many were wounded, and much property was destroyed. The town was almost annihilated.

Isaac Goings was lodged in jail at Mound City, Ill., July 15, on a charge of attempting to murder an old colored man named Venable. His father is in jail on a charge of attempting to outrage his 17-year-old daughter.

The English reserve squadron, under command of the duke of Edinburg, has been off Kiel, Prussia, which was be-decked with flags in honor of the event.

Frank Brown and Jesse Meyers, the last of the gang of five desperadoes who carried on robbery and murder with a high hand in New Madrid county, last winter and during the spring, were hanged at New Madrid Friday, July 15.

George Nantz tried to kill an old man named George Shotwell, at Waukegan, Ills., July 15. A pocket-book saved Shotwell's life from the assassins knife.

Atlanta Constitution:—"Beecher is about to flee to the mountains to nurse his hay fever, but Conkling plays upon his catarrh in his native state."

Eight or nine men, the number is variously stated, robbed a train on the Chicago, Rock Island & Pacific railroad, near Winston, Daviess county, Mo.. Friday night, July 15. They got on at Cameron, and began operations at the point above stated. Conductor Westfall was brutally murdered, and a passenger, named Miller, was also killed. The express safe was robbed, but it contained very little, some $1 600,$1,000 of which was in incontrovertible paper, so that the robbers really got but $600. If they intended to rob the passengers they were prevented by a brakeman, who pulled the air brake and stopped the train, when the outlaws became alarmed and took to flight. There is great excitement in the locality of the crime, and every effort is being made by the officers of the law to capture the thieves.

Gov. Roberts, of Texas, is the only executive officer of a state so far who has refused to join in naming a day for thanksgiving at the recovery of President Garfield. He says he cannot mix up church and state by ordering a day of prayer, &c. We do not doubt the gentleman's sincerity, but think that in his endeavor to stand very straight he leans back just a little. No one asked him to order prayers, only to fix a day that those so disposed might collectively render thanks to Almighty God that an American president was not permitted to die by the hand of an assassin.

NEWS FROM OUR NEIGHBORS.
Complaint is made of scarcity of water in East Nashville.

Foxes among the henneries of suburban Montgomeryites.

Two colored boys, William Stephens and Willie Brooks, "went fighting" in Nashville Monday night, during which the latter was seriously, if not fatally, stabbed by the former.

The favorable report on the bill to appropriate $20,000 for rebuilding the North Georgia Agricultural College, at Dahlonega, will probably secure its passage without serious opposition.

At Birmingham, Alabama, Mrs Lockhart poured coal-oil on the wood in order to make a fire. The fire reached the can, the can exploded, and the lady and one of her children were burned to death.

Friday morning at 1 o'clock a large body of masked men appeared at the jail in Paris, Kentucky, and demanded the prisoner Jim Offutt, but the jailer had made his escape with the keys. The city was aroused and the mob foiled.

While the family of Perry Lawler, colored, were seated in their cabin on the Jehu Lawler place, in Madison county, Alabama, Tuesday evening of last week, lightning descended and killed the wife of Perry Lawler and a son more than half-grown.

There were 750 distilleries in operation in the United States last year. Of this number, 254 were in Kentucky. North Carolina had a greater number than Kentucky, but Tennessee makes more fine whisky than all the other States of the Union combined.

Four colored men murdered a negro woman two or three days ago near Walnut Grove, Georgia. Their trial has just taken place at Monroe, and strange to say, after a full investigation they were discharged on the ground that the killing was done in self-defense.

The fragmentary portions of the body of a negro were found on a curve, a short distance south of Carter's Creek Station, on the Cincinnati Southern railway, Tuesday morning. The man was supposed to have gone to sleep on the track and was run over by several freight-trains during the night. His body had been torn to fragments, and these and blood were strewn along the road for some distance. He was so badly used up that he could not be identified.

A. R. E. Zuker, an architect, and Hugh Wilson, of Meridian, Mississippi, met on the street Tuesday afternoon, when Zuker asked Wilson to retract some remark Wilson had made against him, when Wilson replied that he would retract in this way, striking Zuker in the eye, breaking his spectacles and cutting his nose. Wilson pulled his derringer, putting it within a few inches of Zuker's breast, but it snapped. Zuker then pulled his, when Wilson ran. Zuker firing at him three times, one shot taking effect in his leg; one shot grazed a bystander's face.

Frankfort (Ky.) Yeoman, August 2d: "The dying of large numbers of fish in the river at this point is quite noticeable, and many persons are disposed to attribute the mortality to the large quantity of distillery slops emptied into the river; but we are not altogether satisfied with this explanation, since there is no visible reason why the fish should not have been dying from the same cause for the last six months. The slop, after all, is nothing but cornmeal with its spirit extracted, and if any deleterious elements attend it, why have not the fish been dying every day instead of all at once? There must be some other cause which science has not yet discovered. The occasional dying of fish in lakes, ponds and rivers upon which there are no distilleries has been observed for years. Might not the poisoned dogs thrown into the river have something to do with it?"

Mason Ball, of Mason county, aged 71 years, will bet $1,000 that he can walk 50 miles in a day.
With the recovery of the President, all kinds of stock are advancing to their former worth.
Lapham's term will expire in the U. S. Senate March 4th, 1885, and Miller's two years later.
Kentucky is out annually $100,000 for the support of pauper idiots and lunatics outside of Asylums.
Not more than ten men were killed in the State on election day. This is a wonderful improvement.
W. G. Fargo, of Wells, Fargo & Co., organizers of the American Express, died at Buffalo Wednesday.
A monument to the Confederate dead was unveiled at the cemetery in Culpeper, Va., a few days since.
The government has netted a revenue of $715,269.39 during the last twelve months on cigarettes alone.

—Hon. J. C. Burch, Clerk of the U. S. Senate, died in Washington last Thursday night. He was a Tennesseean.
—"The great unhung," as the Lexington Press calls Jas. H. Arnold, is dishonoring the State again with his presence.
—Senator Ben Hill, of Georgia, has just been operated on for cancer of the mouth, which he says was caused by smoking.
—Old General Merriwether was again elected to the Legislature in Jefferson county. He will be the oldest man in the body.
—Sitting Bull and his braves have surrendered, and have safely landed at the retreat provided for them, near Fort Yates, Dakota.
—A Florida school teacher has sent a bundle of hickory switches to Washington, with a request that they be used on Guiteau.

—At Millersburg, last Thursday, the distillery of Josh Barton burned, with 4,000 bushels of wheat and all the machinery. No insurance.
—By means of his new appliance, the induction balance, Prof. Bell has discovered that the ball in the President's body is located within the abdominal erea.
A keeper of a low saloon, named Steele, shot and killed Policeman Hendricks in Lexington on Monday, because he went in to arrest a disorderly negro.
The children of R. E. Little entered suit Saturday in the Jefferson Court of Common Pleas against James H. Arnold for $50,000 damages in killing their father.
The steamboats Idlewild and Osceola were destroyed by fire at the Memphis wharf Sunday night. Loss, $45,000. The fire originated in the lamp room of the Idlewild.
Samuel White, a cripple living near Florence, South Carolina, outraged his married sister, and afterward waylaid, shot and killed her husband. He was arrested, and is now in jail.

jim-chutt-paris-1881-08.A5:
Killed His Brother-in-law,
Paris, Ky., August 24—Yesterday Wm. H. Corrert killed a notorious desperado, James S. Offutt, his brother-in-law. Offutt had threatened Corrert's life with a shot gun before his very door and had thrown Mrs. Corrert into spasms and caused her death. This was Corrert's retribution.
jim-chutt-paris-1881-08.A7:
A DESPERADO KILLED.
PARIS, Kv., Aug. 24.—Yesterday afternoon James S. Offutt was killed by William H. Current, near the latter's residence, at Ewalt's Crossroads. Offutt was perhaps the most noted and desperate man in the Blue Grass Region, and Current and Offutt were brothers-in-law, the latter having married about a year since. Some weeks ago an altercation between Current and Offutt caused a desire on the part of the latter for the life of the former. Armed with a shotgun, Offutt went to Current's house, and by threats of killing her husband so excited Mrs. Current that she was thrown into spasms, and from the effects of these, coupled with the sickness attendant upon premature childbirth, she died.

A TEXAS TRAGEDY.

SHERMAN, Tex., Aug. 24.—The news of a most horrible affair in Cook County has been received. Some time since Bon Blanton, ex-Sheriff of Cook County, and a despotate man, met James Todd, who had been a witness against him in a lawsuit, and abused and insulted him in a most outrageous manner. Thoy separated, each vowing to meet the other for a final settlement. The men met to-day and both drew weapons and fired. Todd was shot through the heart and in the breast. The top of Blanton's head was blown off. Both men were lying dead when discovered.

A MURDERER EXTRADITED.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

EAST SAGINAW, Mich., Aug. 24.—On June 27, 1876, in Simcoe County, Ontario, Henry McCormick killed John Hangman in a quarrel at a logging-bee. McCormick fled the country, and a month ago was found on a backwoods farm in Midland County and brought to this city, where the examination took place, and the depositions were forwarded to Washington, application having been made for extradition. The papers arrived from Washington yesterday ordering unconditional extradition, and an officer from Toronto will start for Canada to-morrow with the prisoner.

ESCAPE OF A LIFE CONVICT.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

LINCOLN, Neb., Aug. 24.—A life convict named Foster escaped from State Prison last night. He was regarded as trusty and drove a prison team. He did not report at the usual hour last night, and the team was found tied to a tree and the man gone. No reliable clue has yet been discovered. His crime was the shooting of a negro at Nebraska City about twelve years ago.

SHOTOUNS.
JOHNSTON, Edgefield Co., S. C., Aug. 24.—A terrible tragedy occurred about ten miles from this place to-day between J. W. Huzzard and his son and J. W. Timmerman, in which Timmerman was killed and Buzzard and son seriously wounded. An old foul was the cause of the attack. The weapons used were double-barreled shotguns.

COLD-BLOODED MURDER.

Toleno, O., Aug. 24.—John Herman, a livery-stable keeper, and formerly City Marshal of Deshler, O., was shot and instantly killed at that place to-night by Peter Cole, a drayman. The killing is the result of a long-standing foul between the two men. Colo was arrested and brought to this city to-night.

A MINNESOTA MURDER.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
DuLurie, Minn., Aug. 24.—The man Enoch Hallom, who was shot by Franz Larmlere last Saturday night in a house of ill-fame, died at 19 last night from the wound. The murderer made good his escape.

SOLDIERS' REUNION.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
Kokomo, Ind., Aug. 24.—The soldiers' reunion started out to-day with the most flattering prospects of being a grand affair. Al-

ready there are fifty tents on the ground, 500 breech-loading rifles, and three pieces of artillery. Two companies of fifty men each, all soldiers from Sharpsville and Russlaville, this county, reported to-day. To-morrow the crowd will arrive. Companies from Peru, Logansport, and Muncie will arrive on the morning strain. To-morrow afternoon the uniformed rank of the Knights of Pythias, No. 6, the boys who won the laurels from Chicago at Lafayette, will give an exhibition drill, and on Friday the sham battle will be fought. The following are the officers: T. M. Kirkpatrick, Commanding officer of the Post; J. E. Kirk, Post Adjutant; A. C. Bennet, Chief of Artillery, Georgo Manson, Gen. Gibson of Ohio, and Gen. Gresham of Indianapolis, are expected to be present during the remaining days of the reunion, and will address the Boys in Blue. The business-houses and the residences all over the city are handsomely decorated, and our city is in holiday attire to welcome the Boys in Blue.

At the Veterans' reunion to-day, Gov. Plaisted made a speech of welcome to the soldiers and sailors, and was followed by Gen. O. O. Howard, ex-Gov. Washburn, and others. Resolutions of condolence and sympathy with the President were passed, and forwarded to Washington.
jim-chutt-paris-1881-08.A10: Sometime ago a desperado named Jim Offutt went to the house of Wm. Current, in Bourbon, during his absence, and by threats that he would kill him on sight, so frightened his wife that she was thrown into spasms, from which she died. Offutt, after some difficulty, was arrested and lodged in jail at Paris, where a mob assembled one night to lynch him, but it was frightened off by the prompt action of the jailer. Afterwards he was allowed bail in the sum of two thousand dollars, which he secured. Tuesday Offutt and Current met in the road. Offutt drew his pistol, but Current was too quick for him, and got in a fatal shot ahead of him. Thus has died one of the worst men that ever lived in that section, and the people rejoice that his end has come. The law hardly ever punishes such fellows, but sooner or later justice overtakes them in a manner far more effective.

A Cowardly Murder.
ON January 14th — A. Ste
Tucson, January 14th.—A Star special from Charleston says that P. Schneider, Chief Engineer of the Tombstone Mill and Mining Company, was to-day shot and instantly killed by a man called "Johnny Behind the Deuce." The murderer tried to force a quarrel at the dinner-table, but failing in this he went out, secreted himself behind the wall of a corral, and when Schneider was passing up to the mill sprang out and shot him through the head. The villain tried to escape, but was shortly arrested. Deceased was highly esteemed by all who knew him.
john-call-tombstone-1881-01-14.A3:
young man named P. Rourke shot and killed P. Schneider, engineer of the Tombstone Company's mill near Charleston. He was at once arrested and taken to Tombstone, and from that place brought to the Tucson jail by Marshal Sippy and Constables Westfuller, Virgil Earp and George McKelvey. The details of the affair, as telegraphed from Charleston last night, are as follows:

About half past twelve o'clock today P. Schneider, the Chief Engineer of the Tombstone Mill and Mining Company, at this place, was eating dinner at a hotel, when a petty gambler, known as "Johnny behind the deuce," and himself had a few words. Johnny behind the deuce then left the table and went out, coming back again in a few minutes armed with a revolver, and told Schneider that he would fix him when he (Schneider) came out.

Not satisfied with this, he again returned, making use of the same expressions. He then left the hotel a second time, and walked about fifty yards from the house, waiting at the corner of a corral. Mr. Schneider, after eating his dinner, walked down past the corral, when Johnny, pulling out his pistol, met Schneider. Schneider, seeing the pistol, said to him, "Go away from me, and let me alone. I don't know you, and was not even talking to you at the table."

Johnny then advanced a step or two and called Schneider several names, and raising his postol deliberately shot him, the ball passing through the head, killing him instantly. The murderer then dropped his pistol and ran about fifty yards to the river, when he was caught by Constable McKelvey. Constable Bell immediately got a spring wagon, and with Constable McKelvey and another man, armed with a shot-gun, drove off as they could for Tombstone.

A CITIZEN reporter visited Rourke at the jail to-day, and found him to be a rather prepossessing young man, who gave his age as "nineteen next April," and stated that he is a miner by occupation; that he has been in the Territory about three years, having been around Tombstone for the last two years, and that prior to going there he had been a porter at the Palace Hotel for a short time. He is rather under the average size, has a fair face, slight black mustache and well-marked eyebrows, blue eyes and black hair, and seemed quiet and self-possessed. He gave the reporter the following account of the affair, which will be found to differ very materially from that given above.

"I didn't know Schneider very well, and I never had spoken a dozen words to him before this affair happened. I went into Smith's restaurant at noon to get lunch. I had been drinking a few glasses of beer, but was sober enough to know what I was about. After I got through eating I went to the fire-place to light a cigar. Schneider made a remark that I thought was intended to be insulting—at least it had that manner—that it must be cold. 'Yes,' I says, 'it is cold.' Then Schneider says, 'I ain't talking to you. Well, says I, you're a little too smart, anyhow.' I got up and started to go out, and Schneider jumped up and made a break at me as if he was going to strike me, and called me a, d——d——d——. Bob Petty was there and he jumped up and caught hold of Schneider and made him sit down. There were some ladies in the restaurant, and it made me awful mad to be called that. I told him that I had too much respect for the ladies to fight him in there, but to come out on the sidewalk. I went out and started down street, and Bob came out and spoke to me. I said to him, 'It was better, anyhow, Bob; I didn't want any trouble with him.' While we were talking, the telegraph operator came out and said, 'Why, that old fellow is crazy.' I said, 'Well, let's go down to the saloon and take a drink.' We started off for the saloon, and Schneider caught up to us at the corner of the corral. I looked around and said, 'I don't want you to throw out any more insults to me.' He says, 'I wasn't talking to you.' I said, 'Well, that's all right, then, if you wasn't.' 'Supposing I was,' says Schneider, 'what are you going to do about it?' I says, 'I ain't a-going to do anything about.' Schneider seemed to get mad, and kept coming nearer and nearer. I kept stepping back, and finally he got close I put my left hand against him, as he got nearer. I said, 'Go away from me; I don't want any trouble with you,' He had a knife in his hand. I was excited, of course, for the man was twice as big as I was. I'm not certain whether the knife was open or not, for his hand was sideways to me, and I could only see the end of the handle. He continued to crowd against me, and I pulled my gun,' [here Rourke made a motion as if to draw, in illustration, the reporter supposed, of his account] ' and shot him. I was so excited when

they would hold an inquest on Schneider, and if I killed him, they would hang me in twenty minutes. I told them that I did kill him, but I wanted a fair trial. Well, I guess you know all the rest."

The murdered man seems to have been universally liked. Richard Gird, Superintendent of the mine, who went to California on last night's train, told Marshal Sippy in the train that Schneider was a quiet, peaceable man, and he never heard of his ever having trouble with anybody before. Mr. Gird admitted, however, that Schneider had a clasp-knife in his hand when he died, but that it was not open.

George McKelvey, the constable who arrested Rourke, had the utmost difficulty in getting him to Tombstone. He had the prisoner in a buggy, and the pursuers nearly caught them at one time. Arrived there, the prisoner was taken to Jim Vogan's saloon, and a strong guard placed over him. Shortly afterward a mob collected and would undoubtedly have hung the prisoner but for the firmness of Marshal Sippy and the other officers. Another buggy was procured and Sippy and Deputy Sheriff Behan got into it, with Rourke between them, and rode off accompanied by fifteen men well armed with rifles, the latter accompanying them a distance of twelve miles. Threats were made that advantage would be taken of the cut-off between Tombstone and Pantano, to reach the latter place on horseback, and the train boarded by the angry vigilantes, but the officers arrived safely with their prisoner, who had about as narrow an escape from death as often falls to the lot of ordinary mortals.

The Charleston Homicide.
The examination of Mike Rourke for the killing of Schneider at Charleston, on Friday, will be held before Judge Neugass as soon as the witnesses can be brought from the scene of the shooting. The accumulating evidence is more and more corroborative of Rourke's own story, as published in Saturday's Citizen, in which case those newspapers which called loudly for the prisoner's gore should feel rather "cheap." More particularly the Tombstone Epitaph, which published a most ridiculously furious and improbable account of the affair. There is too much inexcusable killing in this county, but if the statements of the arresting officers are to be credited, there are a dozeu men in our county jail who deserve lynching much more than does young Rourke.

CONTESTED ELECTION.

Paul, the defeated Republican candidate for Sheriff, has commenced a contest suit against Sheriff Shibell, his competitor, and it drags its weary length along in the First District Court. It is novel in its character, one witness for the contestant to-day swearing that while he was a Judge of Election at San Simon he stuffed the ballot box with over a hundred votes. It looks a little thin; but, in the meantime, Sheriff Shibell is on the inside and has most of the advantages.

MURDEROUS WORK.

Hardly had the murderer been started for Tucson when a peripatetic soap peddlar stabbed a faro dealer of Tombstone so that he may die. It seems to be a carnival of murder, and the assassin stalks boldly over the land. We have a
