john-call-tombstone-1881-01-14.A10:
KILLING OF SCHNEIDER AT CHARLESTON.
People Out There Think It a Cruel Murder.
This homicide has occasioned much indignant feeling, especially at Charleston. After time enough has elapsed for any sudden passion to subside, the feeling is but little abated. A friend of ours has received a letter from a reliable man and resident of Charleston of date 22d instant, from which we are permitted to make the following extracts:

As nearly as the facts can be gathered at this date—eight days after the killing—they are these: June 14, Schneider went to a restaurant kept at Stillwell's corral, where he was accustomed to get his meals, for his lunch, at about 1:30 p. m.. On entering Mr. Lindsay, telegraph operator at this place, spoke to him about the weather being cool or something of the kind, and Schneider answered him. Rourke was in the room, and pretending that Schneider was addressing him, said something insulting to Schneider, who replied that he did not know him (Rourke) and would have nothing to do with him. Thereupon Rourke said he did not like a Dutch s—— of a b—— anyway, etc., which made Schneider very angry, and he made a rush at him, but was stopped by Petty, who was with Rourke at the time. Rourke and Petty then went out, Rourke remarking that he would fix Schneider when he came out, etc. Petty and Rourke were sleeping in a room connected with the restaurant, and it is supposed that Petty went into the room, got his pistol and gave it to Rourke, as the pistol belonged to Petty. The two went to the corner of the corral where Schneider must necessarily pass. After finishing lunch he started toward the mill and was stopped by them. A few words were spoken, Schneider urging them all the time to leave him alone, that he wanted nothing to do with him (Rourke.) Rourke then advanced toward Schneider, pulled the pistol and fired, the ball striking him in the face and causing instant death. All of the good people, and in fact everyone in Charleston, unite in pronouncing it an unprovoked and most cruel murder, and hope that the prisoner will be punished as he deserves. An effort was made to hang the prisoner, but he was hurried off and thus escaped what he richly deserved.

The following unique description of the manner in which a Berrien county farmer recently broke an ox we get from the Alapaha News: "A gentleman in our town, well known for his industry and manly deportment, undertook a few days since to plow an ox. Everybody who has had any experience in working the horned beast know that they possess more contrariness and hard headedness to the square inch than all other animals combined. The horned horse was harnessed and hitched to the plow without manifesting any unwillingness whatever to perform the work, but when the word go was given he kicked up his heels and waltzed around a time or two on his fore feet, and came down with his head towards the plow. Every effort to get him in position resulted in his performing a similar feat, and the gentleman was pondering in his mind the propriety of taking to the fence, when the idea occurred to him to whip the ox in the face, whereupon the unattended animal ran backwards, dragging the plow, guided by the plowman, and thus the work was accomplished, but 'ge' and 'ha' were entirely left out of the programme."

John W. Mackay.

New York, December 2d.—John W. Mackay is in town, and may be seen daily at the Bank of Nevada. He sails for Europe on the 14th instant. He says there is nothing for him to do in this country, and he might as well enjoy himself abroad. There were no new developments in the Comstocks; the company had lost $4,000,000 the past two years, and there was nothing in view at present of sufficient importance to keep him in California.

The Landing of Foreign Criminals.

New York, December 2d.—Collector Robertson to-day notified the Captain of the steamer St. Germain that Carl Benjamin Kendal, a confirmed criminal, shipped by his vessel to America by the authorities of Bothinger, Switzerland, would be refused permission to land. If he landed clearance would be refused the vessel. Robertson acted under the statute forbidding the landing of criminals.

Iowa Free Traders.

Des Moines, December 2d.—A number of gentlemen of both political parties, from various parts of the State, met last evening and took preliminary steps toward the organization of a new State Free Trade League. They concluded their labors to-day, and organized a new Partisan League, with O. Mosher, President; C. E. Russell, Vice-President; H. Philpot, Secretary; S. W. Goode, Treasurer. The organization provides for three classes of members: First, a Central League of limited membership; second, empowered to organized branch Leagues, and third, an unlimited reading membership, lasting one year, and entitling its members to all the literature of the Society. The headquarters of the League are at Des Moines, and there was great unanimity of sentiment, and a firm purpose was manifested to make a vigorous entry into the contest for free trade.

The Connection of the Two Great Southern Railroads.

TUCSON, December 2d.—A Star special from Sierra Blanco, Texas, says: The two great railroads were connected at 4 P. M. yesterday at Sierra Blanco, beyond El Paso, thus making another through line to the East. In 1869 when the first overland connection was made, James Campbell was Superintendent on the Central Pacific at Promontory, and A. M. Hoxie was Superintendent on the Union Pacific Railroad. November, 1881, they met again to connect the southern route at Sierra Blanco, thus shaking hands across the point of time from 1869 to 1882.

Riot in an Alabama Mining Town.

DECATUR (Ala.), December 2d.—A riot occurred yesterday at Ansmith, a mining town in this State, in which many colored men took part, using stones and pistols. The policemen, in an attempt to restore order, shot and killed two negroes. The policemen were arrested and exonerated.

Fatal Shooting Affray.

GADSDEN (Ala.), December 2d.—In an affray here Buck Martin was mortally shot by a man named Williams. He returned the fire and instantly killed Williams. Martin died to-day.

Robbed by Negroes—Beaten to Death.

DAWSON (Ga.), December 2d.—Near this place yesterday John E. Moreland was assaulted and robbed by three negroes. Mart. Thompson, supposed to be one of the robbers, was captured by white men, and is reported to have been beaten to death. No traces of Thompson can be found, but a piece of a bloody shirt and socks buried in a swamp.

Three Girls Burned to Death.

DESMOINES (Ia.), December 2d.—The Register's special from Winteret says: The dwelling of J. J. Furrow, three miles southwest of here, was burned last night at midnight. Three girls sleeping up stairs, aged 9, 12 and 17, were burned to death. Their bodies were completely charred. The children were wakened, but were afraid to jump.

The Former Home of President Madison.

ORANGE COURT-HOUSE (Va.), December 2d.—Montpelier, formerly the home of President Madison and his burial place, was sold yesterday by auction for $19,000.

DENVER, December 2d.—A Republican Trinidad special says: A fight between three Mexicans and two cowboys on a ranch near here, resulted in Dutchy Brown receiving a fatal wound, W. B. Cartright two slight wounds, and one Mexican two shots in the breast. The Mexicans escaped.

A Working Majority Assured.
MILWAUKEE, December 2d.—A cablegram from Congressman Deuster, received to-day, states that he cannot leave Hamburg before to-morrow, and does not expect to arrive in Washington before December 15th. This gives the Republicans a working majority in the House.

Subsidence of the Kansas Bank Exciture.
CALDWELL (Kansas), December 2d.—The excitement over the failure of the banks has subsided. Danford's wife is now with him. It is expected that matters will be satisfactory arranged shortly.

War of Races.
BRADFORD (Pa.), December 2d.—In a riot among 100 drunken Swede and Irish workmen on the railroad, a Swede named Brandt was killed and three others fatally wounded.

Verdict of Acquittal.
DETROIT, December 2d.—The jury acquitted Mrs. Barnard, on trial for the murder of the wife of Rev. E. Curtis, by setting fire to her clothes. The case has been very mysterious.

The Dairy Convention.
CEDAR RAPIDS (Ia.), December 2d.—The Dairy Convention adjourned to day, after taking important and decisive action on the questions before it.

MONDAY, SEPTEMBER 5, 1881.
THE NEWS THIS MORNING.
FOREIGN.—Three Irish state prisoners are in the infirmary of Kilmainham jail; Mr. Lowell is said to have asked for a special medical examination in case of one of them.

DOMESTIC.—The President passed a comfortable day yesterday, though in the course of Saturday night he vomited twice; his removal, it is thought, will take place on or before Tuesday morning. ——— The news of the massacre by Apaches of General Carr's command is confirmed; Fort Apache was attacked by the savages; other outrages were committed by Indians near the Mexican border. ——— The Court of Inquiry in the case of the naval officers who were killed at Newport by the explosion of a torpedo has been convened. ——— A negro was shot at a camp meeting near Uniontown, Penn. ——— Counterfeit nickels, made by prisoners in an Ohio Penitentiary, have been discovered. ——— The Freethinker's National Convention at Hornellsville, N. Y., adjourned.

CITY AND SUBURBAN.—Ex-Secretary Evarts yesterday gave a TRIBUNE reporter his views about the results of the Monetary Conference. ——— Many sermons were preached about the condition of the President and the results of it. ——— Details of a bold robbery in Harlem were made public. ——— Many persons went to the pleasure resorts despite clouds and a light breeze.

THE WEATHER—TRIBUNE local observations indicate cloudy or partly cloudy weather, with higher temperature and increased possibilities of rain late in the day. Thermometer yesterday: Highest, 70°; lowest, 65°; average, 67°8°.

ALEXIS' OBSERVATIONS IN FAYETTE COUNTY.
UNIONTOWN, September 7th.

UNIONTOWN, September 7th.
Since writing our former letter we have left Moore's works and are sojourning along the route of the new railroad from Uniontown to Brownsville. The road is now being graded and we are told that work is going on all along the line. There are a great many persons working on the route who are from West Virginia—Some from old Monongalia, and some from Preston. Mr. E. Trickett, of Gladesville is one of the bosses—and he is a good one. They want to complete the road this fall. This road is laid out through a coal country. A company formed for the purpose has bought nearly all the coal lands along the route. Wm. Hough sold his farm, which is two miles from Uniontown, and contains 161 acres, for $40,000, which is just $27,000 more than he gave for it two years ago.
The Monongahela Association of the Regular Baptist Church met at Uniontown last week. Their ministers occupied the various pulpits of the town last Sunday, both morning and evening.

The colored folks held a camp meeting near Moore's Works last week. It broke up Sunday night in a row between some of the darkies and white rowdies. Several of the parties were shot and others cut. The whites came out victorious. One negro was chased four miles and finally shot in the back. ALEXIS.

robert-garnes-marysville-1881-01-18.A1:
CRIMINAL NEWS. Horrible Triple Murder Near the Little Village of Plain City, O. An Old Lady 90 Years Old, Her Niece, and a Boy, the Victims. Murderous Attack, by a Baltimore Belle upon the President of a Bank. The Viskow Murder and Suicide—A Young Man Kicked to Death. Detroit the Scene of a Grave-Robbery The Body Found in a Medical College. Two Americans Murdered at a Mexican Fandango, and Their Bodies Burned. A TRIPLE TRAGEDY. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
Mrs. Ophelia Clark, situated about three miles from Plain City, near the boundary lines of Franklin, Madison, and Union Counties, were committed last night three murders under one roof. Mrs. Ophelia Clark was a colored woman who many years ago lived in this city, and by hard work saved up a sum of money with which she purchased a small farm and home, which last night was invaded and her life taken, together with that of her niece and a young colored boy, aged about 14, who had been adopted by Mrs. Clark.

THE ENTIRE FAMILY consisted of Mrs. Clarke and her two nieces and the small boy. The girls' names were Maria and Matilda Scott. It appears that during the past year Mrs. Clarke had leased her farm to a colored man by the name of Robert Garnes, but, owing to his aspirations in becoming on too familiar terms with one of the nieces, Mrs. Clarke saw fit to dispense with his services, and a short time since engaged another man to carry on the farm. It is said that this was a severe blow to Garnes, who remained in the neighborhood. Last night one of the girls, in company with some of the neighbors, went to spend the evening with friends a mile or two distant, leaving at

THE FARM-HOUSE the old lady, Mrs. Clarke, who was nearly blind with age, her sister Maria, and the little boy, named Charles Goode, all well, contented, and happy. At about midnight she returned, and upon opening the door of the house a scene of the most horrible character met her gaze. Lying upon the floor at full length, directly in front of the door, covered with blood, lay the lifeless body of the boy, while a scene of confusion was apparent on all sides, the tables and furniture overturned, and an armful of wood lying in the middle of the floor in the front room.

HORRIFIED BY THE SCENE,
the young girl screamed for help, which attracted the attention of the boy and another girl who were just departing. Returning to the house and hearing no sounds, lights were secured, after which a still more horrid spectacle, if possible, presented itself. In an adjoining room, and lying in a pool of blood, with the brain oozing out from the right side of her head was found the lifeless body of Maria Scott. The bedding was half-torn and besmeared with blood, while on the wall were great blotches of bespattered blood and brains. In another room, lying partly upon the floor and a sofa,

ANOTHER HORRIBLE SIGHT
was met. There, with her head crushed in, was found the dead body of the old colored lady, 90 years of age. A pool of blood had already formed upon the floor, and so recent had the fatal blow been struck, the purple stream had not yet ceased to flow. In all parts of the house were the evidences that a terrible struggle had taken place. The little boy, Charles Goode, had evidently struggled hard to escape from the horrible death which awaited him, for his clothing was torn into shreds, and both arms broken in his herole struggles. Lying near, upon the floor, was found

A PIECE OF HIS SKULL
measuring three inches long by two wide, leaving the brain without a cover. Two large bruises were also found, one over each eye. As soon as possible the boy who had brought the young lady home was dispatched to arouse the neighbors and spread the news that a whole family had been murdered. Who this triple murder was committed by can better be determined by following the suspected one. At the early hour of 4 o'clock this morning, Robert Garnes, the colored man who had heretofore conducted the affairs on the farm of Mrs. Clarke, presented himself at the telegraph office at Plain City, the nearest telegraph station, and desired to send a message to the friends of the family at Cincinnati and Columbus. He reported that there had been

A THIRD MURDER
committed, but, upon being closely questioned by the officers, he became confused and told several conflicting stories of the affair. A number of citizens and officers, accompanied by the negro, at once started for the spot, and then the horrible nature of the crime was fully realized. Everything was confusion. Nothing had been touched until the officers visited the house. Physicians were summoned, and by them it was discovered that

AN OUTRAGE HAD BEEN ATTEMPTED
upon the person of Maria Scott before the murder of any of the inmates had been attempted. Garnes was closely examined, and blood was found upon several parts of his clothing, while his face and neck showed the marks of a conflict. Upon close examination blood was also found upon his underments, and, in fact, circumstances were so strongly against him that his arrest soon followed. The little boy who had been dispatched to spread the alarm states that when but a little distance from the house he was stopped by Garnes on the road and

THREATENED WITH DEATH
should he raise any alarm whatever, and fearing for his life he returned home. From the developments brought out by the investigation to-day, it is believed that Garnes, finding that a portion of the family were absent, visited the farm-house last night, and being unsuccessful in accomplishing his purpose attempted to rape Miss Marla, when a terrible struggle took place. It is believed that before making this attack he had succeeded in inducing the boy Goode to go after wood, which would leave him in comparative safety in the accomplishment of his design.

THE SCREAMS OF THE YOUNG WOMAN,
it is believed, attracted the old lady, Mrs. Clarke, to the room where she was found. The theory is that the boy Goode entered the room with his arms full of wood after the attempted rape had been folled, and that he was at once attacked by Garnes, from whom he was successful in escaping to an inner room, where he was killed, and where a portion of his jacket and some trinkets which fell from his pocket were found. The first evidences of

THE HORRIBLE WORK
that had been done in the old farm-house

when the officers visited the place this morning was the finding on the outside near the door of a long wooden shovel red with the blood of the murdered victims within. Miss Scott states that after she arrived at home, and found that the family were murdered, she could not find any trace of a living soul about the horse, and was certain that Garnes was not there. That he should have known of the horrible affair and not have been present is regarded as

EVIDENCE OF HIS QUIT.

Hundreds of people from the surrounding country have visited the scene of the horrible butchery of last night. Excitement during the day has run high, and threats of lynching have been freely indulged in, and would have doubtless been carried into effect by the colored people of the vicinity had they been headed by a leader. But the counsel of the officers and the white people had the effect of holding back those who were eager to administer justice on the spot. In fact, a rope had been secured, and at one time it was feared would be brought into use. For safety Garnes was taken to Plain City, from which place he will be at once taken and placed in jail at Marysville, in Union County. Fears are entertained that the Sheriff will have trouble in landing Garnes in jail, as the indictments point strongly in the direction of a summary disposal of the case.

BLOODCURDLING TRIPLE MURDER
Near Plain City-A Horrible Tale-A Mother and Two Children Beaten to Death by a Negro With a Hickory Club.
Near Plain City—A Horrible Tale—A Mother and Two Children Beaten to Death by a Negro With a Hickory Club.

Detroit, Mich., January 18.—A most horrible triple murder was committed near Plain City, Madison county, some time during last evening. This morning Bobert Garner, a colored man, reported that a murder had been committed about three miles east of Idion and wanted to telegraph to certain parties in Cincinnati of the affair. Upon going to the place indicated a horrible sight was revealed. Mrs. Matilda Scott, a widow aged 40 years, her daughter, 22 years old and an adopted son aged 14 and named Charlie Goode, were found on the floor dead, with their brains scattered about the floor and smeared upon the wall of their sleeping room. A large hickory club smeared with blood was found upon the porch near the dead, and it is supposed it was with this bludgeon that the deed was committed. Robert Garner has been arrested, charged with the murder. There are several suspicious circumstances which point to him as the murderer. He lived for six or eight years with the Scott family, but about three months ago left them in anger because they would not rent the farm to him. He was greatly excited when he told the story of the murder at four o'clock this morning, and tells contradictory stories. Mrs. Scott was the owner of a good farm and was reported well-to-do financially among her colored friends, and the terrible manner of her taking off has created much excitement in the usually quiet rural neighborhood where she had lived all her life.

CRIMINAL NEWS.

THE OHIO BUTCHERY.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Columbus, O., Jan. 19.—The intense excitement caused by the unprovoked murder of Mrs. Ophelia Clark, aged 94 years, Miss Marla Scott, aged 22, and Charles Goode, a boy aged 12, near Plain City, on the border line of Franklin, Union, and Madison Counties, on Monday night, still continues, and the entire population of the three counties in that vicinity have thronged around the hours since early yesterday morning, wrought up to a high state of indignation and horror. There is but little to add to the details of the horrible affair telegraphed The Times last night. A close examination of the bodies of the demon's victims show that the murderer must have wielded.

TERRIBLE BLOWS with his instrument of death. Garnes, the alleged murderer, it is well known, was desperately in love with Marla Scott, but his advances had been repulsed. It is stated that Garnes had threatened to get even with the family for what he considered an offront. The entire family were well-to-do, and bore an excellent reputation among the white and colored people in the neighborhood. The stories told by the suspected and probable murderer are so conflicting as to leave little, if any, doubt of his guilt. It required considerable strategy last evening to get Garnes away from the excited crowd to take him to the Marysville jail. He was first taken to Plain City, and then secretly removed by an out-of-the-way route to Marysville.

THE WEAPON USED was an iron bar about three feet long, which was used as a poker for the fire. It has evidently been the handle of an old-fashioned shovel or frying-pan. The head of the old lady was literally beaten into a jelly. The girl's skull was very badly mushed. The alleged murderer, Robert Garnes, has lived in this section of the country about five years. His father, who resided near Hilliard, died about a year ago. His mother and sister still reside at that place. Garnes is a light mulatto, of medium height, and a very muscular man. He is about 24 years of age. He admitted, yesterday, that he tried to outrage Marla Clark last spring, but was not successful.

GARNES WAS DELIVERED TO THE JAIL AUTHORITIES

In Marysville last night about 9 o'clock, and lodged in jail through the back way, as there was a large crowd assembled around the jail awaiting his arrival in town. Had he been taken in the front way, before the excited crowd which was assembled, he would have been lynched; but, as they ran him in secretly and have him lodged in a cell, he may now escape lynching. The better part of the citizens are glad that he is safely lodged in jail, there to await a proper trial. The funerals of the three murdered victims will be held tomorrow morning, and their remains brought to this city and placed in a vault, the friends of the deceased fearing that the grave-robber would make off with them if buried in the cemetery.

A TRAIN LEAVING Elmira on the Erie Road eleven o'clock at night met with a terrible accident near Tioga Center. The driving wheel axel of the locomotive broke while the train was running at the rate of thirty-five miles an hour, and instantly the cars were hurled from the track, some of them turning over two and three times. The postal car immediately took fire, and four postal clerks in the car perished in the flames. In the express car was a messenger, Henry C. Brewer, of Elmira. Efforts were made to relieve him. A hole was cut in a side door of the car, so that he got his head out, but his leg were fastened by a piled up mass of express matter. The train men tried to pull him out, but the flames drove them away. They saw his hair and whiskers burned off, and then he put his hands up to his eyes and fell back into the flames. Five men in all were burned, but no passengers were injured.

A CORRESPONDENT at Marysville, Ohio, under date of Jan. 18, writes: "The most flendish murder ever occurring in this section was perpetrated last night, four miles north of Plain City, in this county. Shortly after dark, Robert Garnes, who lives with a family by the name of Scott, consisting of an old lady aged about ninety years, a young lady aged twenty, and a boy aged sixteen, all colored, went home drunk, and from what can be learned, attempted to rape the girl, and being caught by the other members of the family, he made use of a heavy poker, and killed all three of them. When found late at night they were all cold in death, excepting one, but she died soon after. The murderer was arrested to-day, making no attempt to escape. The excitement in the community is intense, and he was hurried away as quickly as possible. Since dark this evening he was brought here and lodged in jail as quietly as possible. Threats of lynching are freely made, and if any one should head the movement there may be trouble. Sheriff Hobensack will stand by his prisoner to the last, and is doing all he can to prevent an outbreak.

A NEW TELEGRAPH company is organizing in Chicago for the purpose of constructing a line between Chicago and New York City; and eventually, it may be, to other points in the United States, and by a new cable line to Europe. Articles of incorporation have been forwarded to the office of the Secretary of State at Springfield, and a certificate has been granted. The name of the new organization is the Chicago and International Telegraph Company, and its object is declared to be the construction and operation of a telegraph and telephone line between Chicago and New York. The capital stock is $1,000,000, with power to increase to as much larger an amount as may prove to be required. The incorporators and leading movers in this matter are some of Chicago's heaviest capitalists, including N. K. Fairbank, Marshall Field, Perry H. Smith, Geo. L. Dunlap, Henry W. King, George C. Walker, W. T. Crosby, John B. Lyon and others.

OHIO STATE NEWS.
JAMES OGLEBIE was killed at Chillicothe, while coupling cars.

A LEGISLATIVE COMMITTEE is investigating the affairs of the State Reform Farm.

SARA BENHARET played an engagement of four nights at Cincinnati commencing on the 31st ult.

HUGH McGOWEN, of New Hagerstown, slipped, fell and broke his neck, from which he died instantly.

THE Grand Jury of Carroll County returned sixty-one indictments. They are mostly against liquor dealers.

The trial of Thomas Hightower, for the killing of Wm. Newland, last September, is in progress at Kenton.

IDA BRIDWELL, a young girl of good family, who has been living a fast life, suicided at Zanesville last week.

ORMAND BLISS, living ten miles east of London, shot himself in the head with suicidal intent. The wound was not fatal.

At Canton, the Grand Jury indicted Joseph Kline for murder in the first degree. Kline is charged with poisoning his father.

The citizens of Bellefontaine, a few days ago, held a mass-meeting to devise means for the better observance of the Sabbath.

WILLIAM WILCOX, of New California, is in jail for cutting his wife's hand off at the wrist with an ax. The account says he was drunk.

FRANKLIN HOUSTON, a well known and highly esteemed young bachelor of thirty-two years, of Urbana, has been adjudged insane and committed to the Columbus Asylum.

BELLÉFONTAINE people are good feeders. A correspondent says the combined weight of five landlords is 1,294 pounds, and the combined weight of three of them is 900 pounds.

MISS SARAH MITCHELL, a daughter of Hon. Robert Mitchell, of Zanesville, has been adjudged insane. When a girl Miss Mitchell fell into a cistern, since which time epilepsy has gradually developed.

WM. HOSEWORTH, indicted for murder in Marion County, has been granted a change of venue to Hardin County, and his trial set for April 18th, at which time a special term will be called. Bail was refused.

A CORRESPONDENT relates that Dora Sever, a servant in the family of J. C. Bloker, at Sandusky, has slept eight hours without waking. The physicians say the cause is the suffusion of the brain with blood, producing congestion.

A MAN at Newark whose name is not given, attempted to shoot himself, and failing that, tried to hang himself. He was discovered before he departed this life however, and he is now an inmate of the insane asylum.

THE Free Press of Lancaster has been indicted on three counts for criminal libel. The Free Press published a series of articles about the Court and the Court officers, and the Grand Jury says that the matter so published was
dicted on three counts for criminal label. The Free Press published a series of articles about the Court and the Court officers, and the Grand Jury says that the matter so published was libelous.

REV. A. LEHMAN, Presbyterian pastor at Dresden, while attempting to stop a runaway horse attached to a sleigh, was thrown down and stepped upon by the horse. His face was badly mutilated, and a part of his right ear cut off by the horse's hoof.

AT Marysville a special Grand Jury was impaneled to investigate the charges against Gaines, for the triple murder of Ophelia Clark, her niece, Maria Scott, and an adopted son of Mrs. Clark, and returned three indictments against him for murder in the first degree.

ROBERT GILLES, of Zanesville, was coasting after night, and going at a high rate of speed could not, therefore, tell exactly where he was going to land. Well, he had his feet spread apart, and in that way ran right astrraddle of a tree, and it hurt him terribly. He is laid up in consequence.

TWENTY-FOUR young and middle-aged men of Williamsburg, Noble County, were arrested and thrown in jail at Caldwell, by the Sheriff, for playing five-cent-ante, whatever that is. They confessed their guilt to the Grand Jury was what led to their arrest. A fine of $2 and costs was imposed on each man.

REV. W. S. BARTON, recently a teacher in Hocking County, has sued the Board of S. h. o. l. Examiners for damages in the sum of $15,000. for revoking his certificate on the alleged ground of immorality. He claims no immorality was proved against him. The Board say they are in possession of facts that will sustain their course.

JOHN CUMMINS, the farmer in Licking County, says he does not understand why people should make a fuss over the manner in which he punishes his boy. He confesses that he took the boy to the barn and split a sapling, and placed it on the boy's tongue, and drove a tack through the sapling, tongue and all, to keep it in place; he then tied him fast to the manger and administered a most severe beating. He is out on bail.

An accident on the Cincinnati, Mount Vernon and Chicago Railroad near Millersburg last week resulted in the injury of fifteen persons. While rounding a curve the rear car struck a broken rail, resulting in it being thrown down a twenty-five foot embankment, the other cars having passed over safely. Dr. L. Firestone, of Columbus, Louis Garnes, conductor, and Mrs. Lydia Wolf, of Canton, an aged lady, were dangerously injured.

Elliott, however, was too fleet-footed for Beltz and escaped punishment. The correspondent states that Beltz also enlisted his wife and sister for interfering in the match in Mattie's behalf.

A CORRESPONDENT at Newcomerstown writes: "A gentleman from Montana arrived here a few days ago who is now on the hunt of a young man named Millburn, whose life has a touch of romance about it. He was born near Newcomerstown, and when quite young his parents died. He was then adopted by an uncle (his father's brother) who shortly afterward died, whereupon young Millburn was adopted by a family named Howell, which family shortly afterward removed to Indiana. This was about nine years ago, and since that time no trace of the Howell family or young Millburn can be found. The aforesaid gentleman from Montana has been endeavoring to find young Millburn for several years, as he (the boy) is the only surviving heir to a large and rich estate in Montana. He has already spent thousands of dollars in the so far fruitless search, and offers a reward of $2,000 to any person furnishing information as to his whereabouts."

A Missouri Tragedy.
CINCINNATI, O, May 13.—The Republican's Charleston (Mo.) special says four men, Frank Brown Jesse Meyers, James Hamilton and Pat Rhodes visited the house of Wm. Knox, five miles south of New Madrid, last Monday night, with the intention of killing him and his half sister, on account of an old grudge. A man named Coleman was carrying a child and walking the floor in the house, and, mistaking Coleman for Knox, the party fired on him and wounded both him and child. A warrant was issued Tuesday for the arrest of the assassins, and Sheriff Walters with a posse started in pursuit, and overtook them at Bayne's store, five miles south of Sikeston. The men fled to the woods and secreted themselves behind a fallen tree.—When the posse came up they received a volley from the concealed party, and Robt. La Farge was killed. The sheriff's party returned the fire, but receiving a second volley they retired. The desperadoes then robbed the dead body of La Farge of his watch, money and shirt studs and fled. In the evening Pat Rhodes, one of the gang who had been wounded by the sheriff's posse, came in and gave himself up. This morning a party of vigilants took him out and hanged him, and hundreds of men are scouring the country in every direction for the remainder of the party. If caught they will be served as Rhodes was served.

A special dispatch to the Gazette says: 'Robt. Garnes, colored, on trial for a trial for a triple murder committed near Plain City, Ohio, last January. was convicted last night of murder in the second degree, the punishment for which is life imprisonment.'

Where was the Pistol Purchased?

Guiteau stated yesterday to the officers that he purchased the pistol the day before the shooting at the store opposite the Treasury, and the name of O'Meara having been suggested to him, he said he believed that was the name of the storekeeper. Mr. O'Meara yesterday afternoon denied that he had sold such pistol. A party answering Guiteau's description made inquiries for a "British Bull Dog pistol" on the preceding day at the Remington store, corner of 10th and D streets; but was not suited.

Wild Excitement at Wheeling.

Lieut. Clem, U.S.A., who arrived in the city last evening from the west, says that the people in his car first heard the news of the shooting of the President at Wheeling, about a quarter to ten yesterday morning. The excitement at Wheeling was intense. It increased at every station that was reached. The people jumped on board the train and demanded to know something. Everybody was wild with excitement, and denouncing the crime. There was almost a riot along the line of the road, Lieut. Clem says.

Died from the Shock.

Yesterday, Mr. Lucius Palmer, an old gentleman 78 years old, died of nervous shock on hearing the news of the shooting of President Garfield. He will be buried to-day, at Rock Creek cemetery.

A Richmond Man Attacks a Colored Man for Cursing the President.

Officer Kearney took into custody this morning and conducted to police headquarters a white man, a stranger in this city from Richmond, Va.—Samuel Frasler—charged by a colored man named Wm. Tinker with cutting him with a knife. Mr. Frazler denied the charge, and said this colored man was cursing and traducing President Garfield, and he jumped at him to catch him, intending to administer chastisement, when the fellow jumped and tore his clothing. Tinker's coat, pants and shirt were cut but not his skin. The affair occurred at the St. James, opposite the Baltimore and Potomac depot. Frasler was detained for a hearing.

THE NEW YORK PRESS ON THE MURDEROUS DEED.

[Special Dispatch to The Evening Star.]
NEW YORK, July 3.

“Impossible to Ignore the Causes which Led to the Act.”

The Times says: “The President's life was assailed by a wretch who represents as distinctly the evil in our system as President Garfield represents the good. For though the murderer was obviously of a disordered mind, it is impossible to ignore the causes which led immediately to this act and which directed his ill-regulated will to its final aim. He was a disappointed office-seeker, and he linked the bitterness of his present disappointment with the passionate animosity of a faction. His resentment was inflamed and intensified by the assaults upon the President which have been common in too many circles for the past few months. Certainly we are far from holding any party or any section of a party responsible for this murderous act, but we believe it our duty to point out that the act was an exaggerated expression of a sentiment of narrow and bitter hatred, which has been only too freely indulged.”

“The Accursed Spoils System.”

The World says: “The authorities at Washington will do well to “make haste slowly” in accepting the tale of Gutteau's insanity. The man's conduct before and after committing his crime was by no means that of a maniac. He seems to have been hanging about the Presidential residence for some days in quest of an opportunity to shoot the President, and he provided himself before entering the railway
seems to have been hanging about the Presidential residence for some days in quest of an opportunity to shoot the President, and he provided himself before entering the railway station on his attrocious errand with a team of swift horses and a carriage, to which he was making his way as quickly as possible when he was fortunately intercepted by a prompt and resolute officer. It was only after his attempt to escape had been thus frustrated that he called out, 'Yes, I have finished Garfield. Now Arthur is President. I am a stalwart.' The letters which were found upon his person were not the letters of a man otherwise than morally insane. His cold-blooded and hypocritical allusion to the probable Christianity of the President and his utterly brutal allusion to the woman whose husband he meant to murder would scarcely have occurred to a madman. A madman committing a murder under the stress of an insane conviction that he was doing a thing necessay and right to be done would scarcely have wasted words on an attempt to vindicate the deed."

The World adds: "If Gulteau was frenzled into trying to murder the Chief Magistrate of his country by the refusal of that Chief Magistrate to give Gulteau an office, Gulteau should be tried, convicted and punished, not only by way of expiation for his own offense, but as an example to the whole country of the inevitable tendency of the accursed 'spolls' system which has eaten its deadly way so far into the manhood and the morals of the American people."

"Faction's Latest Crime."

The Tribune heads its editorial "Faction's Latest Crime," and says:

"Do the leaders of faction ever intend all the mischief which grows from the wild and desperate spirit which they create, feed and stimulate, week after week? Is it not their constant crime against self-government that, by kindling such a spirit, they send weak or reckless men beyond the bounds of right or reason? This assassin, it seems, was not ignorant that he was trying to kill one President and to make another. His language and letters prove that he knew what he was doing only too well. As "a stalwart of the stalwarts," his passion was intense enough to do the thing which other reckless men had wished were done. So the assassin Booth put into a bloody deed the malignant spite of thousands of beaten rebels. His deed stands in history as the cap sheaf of the rebellion. So the spirit of faction which fired the shots of yesterday gave in that act the most complete revelation of its real character. That political fanaticism has been showing itself before us all in many phases little short of madness. The country has seen the wildest ravings of abuse about the President, and has paid little attention—but not because it thought the men who uttered them insane. It has listened to malignant scandals which it has seemed impossible that sane citizens would utter regarding the Chief Magistrate of their country, but has listened with contempt, fancying that the fanaticism of faction would go no further. But curses and threats are followed at last by murderous shots, and the country starts with horror. Never again will any sane man cry, "I am a Stalwart of the Stalwarts!" Never again will a blind and furious fanaticism of faction seem to sane men a thing to boast of. As Booth ended the rebellion by showing what its real spirit was, so this horrid flash of light, which shows how narrow is the dividing line between faction's frenzy and Mexican assassination, will bring an end, let us hope, to a most shameful phase of partisanship in this country."

Guiteau's Alleged Accomplice.

MR. CULTER DESCRIBES HIM—HIS MOVEMENTS AFTER THE SHOTING.

Mr. Culter, the volunteer stranger witness, who was at the railroad station at the time of the shooting, and saw the two suspicious men in earnest conversation in the depot just before the occurrence, was yesterday taken to the jail for the purpose of identifying Guiteau. He states that when he got there the prisoner was lying on his bed, with the bed clothing over him, and he saw him at great disadvantage. He did not at the first glance think it was the same man, until he put his hand up to stroke his beard in the same peculiar and nervous manner, which he recognized at once. He thinks, however, that he should be dressed in the same clothing he wore at the time of the shooting, and the same hat, which would make considerable difference, and would be only fair. He has no doubt about the identity, but says from the movements of them he is positive that the other man who escaped after the shot was fired was the leading spirit, and was giving the smaller man directions how to proceed. His movements were very quick and nervous. He was a tall man, quite six feet high, dark complexion and dark hair and eyes, the latter being very sharp and restless. This man as soon as the shots were fired went directly up 6th street, increasing his gait as he increased the distance from the scene. Mr. Culter's first thought was that they were pickpockets and he involuntarily placed his hand on his pocketbook in passing them. Mr. Culter is a quiet, honest appearing sort of a man, and is evidently deeply impressed with his story, and says whether or not the bottom facts are ever reached, he will still be of the opinion that this man had at least one confederate. Mr. C. is well known to several highly respectable people in this city, who give him a first-rate name for truth and veracity. He will no doubt prove to be an important witness.

Guiteau's Fear of a Mob.

Detective Miller, who has examined the prisoner, says that the only fear the man entertained was of a mob. His theory is that Guiteau after doing the deed expected to jump into the hack he had hired, go to the jail, and there deliver himself up. His fear was that he would be lynched. "In his insanity," said Detective Miller, "he thought he would reach the jail, and there be in safety until he received protection, as he expected from Vice President Arthur."

A thorough examination made by the secret service men and other detectives has brought out a report made to the authorities that Guiteau was undoubted, y insane, and had neither accomplices or other instigation than his overworked and underbalanced brain.

THE MAN WHO ASSAULTED A BOOT-BLACK FOR CURSING THE PRESIDENT.

Samuel Frasier, a large middle-aged white man, was charged in the Police Court this morning with assaulting a colored boot-black named Wm. Tinker, who testified that he was blacking a gentleman's boots at the St. James Hotel corner, Saturday, and Mr. Frasier asked if the President was dead; and then charged witness with cursing the President, and pulled out a knife and cut at witness several times, cutting his clothing. Officer Kearney testified to arresting the defendant, and that when he was taken to Police Headquarters he said that he would cut the —— heart out of any man that would curse the President. Frasier took the stand and stated that he asked if the President was dead, and the young man said, ——, the President, he ain't as dead as he ought to be. Witness told him that he ought not to talk that way, or somebody would kill him, and Tinker then got abusive and struck at witness with his blacking-box, and witness cut at him with a knife. The court remarked that Mr. Frasier was evidently acting under the general excitement, and he would not hold him to so strict an account as he would under ordinary circumstances, and as there was no serious damage done, he would only fine him $5 or 15 days in jail.

The census bureau has issued a bulletin giving in detail the population of the United States classified by race. It shows the total population to be 50,152,866, of which 43,404,877 are white, and 6,577,151 are colored. The number of colored persons to each 100,000 whites is 15,153, against 14,528 in 1870. The greatest proportion of colored to white is in South Carolina, where three-fifths of the whole are colored. In Louisiana and Mississippi from one-half to three-fifths are colored. In Alabama, District of Columbia, Florida, Georgia, North Carolina and Virginia the colored form one-third to one-half of the total. In Arkansas and Tennessee from one-fourth to one-third of the total population are colored. The least proportion among the former slave States is in West Virginia, where there are only 4,355 to 100,000 whites, and in Missouri where there are but 7,168. In the United States, as a whole, there has been a gain of 625 on an assumed basis of 100,000 whites. The great relative gains during the decade have been made in the South, the former slave-holding States. Of the nine of these States which have gained, eight stand at the head of the list, having made relative gains ranging from 944 to nearly 1,000. The number of Asiatics in the United States is 105,717 and North American Indians 63,122. "Indians not taxed," that is, Indians in tribal relations under the care of the government, are not included in the above.

THE FATE OF A FIEND.
HORRIBLE TRAGEDY IN FLORIDA
A Brutal Negro Kills Three Children and Lies in Wait for Their Father-The Miscreant Promptly Lynched.
JACKSONVILLE, July 5.—The particulars of a most horrible triple murder have just reached here. Sheriff Mickler, of Hernando county, who lives some miles from the court house, having occasion to go there on the 29th ult., left his three children, aged eight, eleven and fourteen years, alone with a negro named King, to whom he had been very kind. The fiend shot and mortally wounded the oldest, then droye the others to the woods and shot the elder dead, cut the throat of the younger and left it also for dead. He then returned, robbed the house of what he could carry and lay in wait for Mr. Mickler, designing to kill him on his return. But neighbors accompanied Mr. Mickler, and the murderer was thwarted.

The two wounded children when found were able to give an account of the terrible affair, though one and perhaps both are now dead. The fiend was captured and confessed the crime. He was hanged in the presence of and with the approbation of two hundred citizens. He died sullen and unrepenting.
unnamed-negro-man-1881-06-29.A3: It would seem that inhumanity, atrocity and cold-blooded, fiendish outrage had reached their climax, in the murder of Sheriff Mickler's three children, in Hernando county, Florida, a few days ago, by Sidney King, a negro boy, seventeen years of age, whom the Sheriff had kindly rescued from the clutches of the law, and entrusted, for a few hours, with the care of his children. The details are of the most horrible character, and while mob law is to be condemned in the strongest terms, it is little wonder that a whole community rose up as one man, pursued, captured and promptly executed the perpetrator.

The coroner held an inquest over his body, and upon his person were found a pistol, razor, pocket knife, eight dice, a piece of bone and a copper cent. His name could not be ascertained, but it is supposed he is the man who was drowned off the schooner Seahorse a month or so ago. His body was buried in the marsh near where it was found. On Saturday night, 2d inst., the Austrian

BARK TEVERE WAS BURNED
to the water's edge. She was lying in the bay at the east end of Horn island, loading at the time, and had in her hold 100 sticks of square timber. The fire was caused by the explosion of a coal oil lamp which was hanging in the cabin, and occurred about 12 o'clock at night. The Tevere was built at Gravasce, Austria, in 1872, was formerly named Tebro, and had her name changed in 1874 to the Tevere. She was in command of Capt. Gladleich, was a 426 ton vessel, and was valued at $11,000. She burned out clean, nothing being left of the hull except the planking and metal sheathing. The hull is still afloat and was towed in Tuesday. The officers and crew escaped. Sunday night

A DIFFICULTY took place on the Front between Messrs. Thos. Percy and William Thompson, during which the latter received a dangerous cut in the left side and another light cut in the right shoulder. Percy was arrested and brought before Squire O. Randall, at the courthouse on Monday, and was sent to jail to awrite further developments of the wounds inflicted, as the one in the side was considered dangerous by the physician. It is supposed Thompson was cut with a pocket knife. Percy received a severe blow on the face, supposed to have been done by Thompson with a bottle. As the case was not investigated we refrain from going into details as to the cause of the affray.

SIX IN A ROW.

Monday morning just before the arrival of the 11:14 a.m. train five white young men and a young negro, coal black, became involved in a fracas on the platform, and had several rounds with their fists and sticks. The young men are from Mobile, and we believe came out here to work in the canning factory. They cursed the negro, and the negro cursed them, which diversity was kept up for a few minutes, when they jumped the negro. He stood his grounds until all bands were separated by Judge Randall. No arrests were made. Monday night the indomitable

JOSEPHUS SPARENBERG
and a man by the name of Cooley got into a fight on the Front above the old hotel, and Sparenberg got slightly cut in the shoulder. Joe was not born to die by the knife or pistol, and is a hard man to kill. No arrests in this case. We also learn that a negro man

WAS COWHIDED
by Mr. Ed. Blalack, the negro having insulted bim, but could not learn the particulars.

NEWS FROM OUR NEIGHBORS.
In May the Alabama Press association will meet at Blount Springs.

At Oxford, Mississippi, Decoration day will be observed on the twenty-sixth instant.

Farming this season in Macon county, Alabama, is badly behind, the Jabor growing source.

At Fort Worth, Texas, last Friday, the residences of Mr. Hein and B. G. Johnson were destroyed by fire. The cause of the fire was accidental.

At Taylor's, Yalobusha county, Mississippi, last week, Henry ibry, a farmer, was killed by a freight train in attempting to jump on it while in motion.

At Hope Hill, near Jackson, Tennessee, last week, Dr. Burrow became the father of triplets, gifts from his wife. Two of the children died in a few days.

On Folsom Island, near Batesville, Arkansas, 200 bushels of corn in pens were destroyed by fire, caught from burning trees and log heaps. The corn belonged to W. F. Kamster.

At Columbia, Tennessee, last week, a thief attempted to enter the residence of Mrs. Lithgow, who seized a pistol and fired three shots at the intruder, who escaped. He was a negro.

Near Milan, Tennessee, a few days since, Zel Packer, a negro desperado, was badly shot by Dan Smith, colored, while the former was attempting to break into the house of the latter.

At Uniontown, Alabama, people who are missed from church on Sunday are hunted up next day by some of the brethren, who inquire the cause of absence. Sickness is the only excuse taken from absentees.

Near Hollywood, Arkansas, John C. Carter, while burning a coal-kiln, heard a burning three crack behind him, and, looking up, saw the tree falling toward him, and at once ran for life, but a limb struck him on the shoulder, kill-

ing him instantly. The same day Mr. Carter had been elected marshal of Hollywood.

Several mad dogs were killed during the past week at Grenada, Mississippi.

Pine Bluff, Arkansas, is agitating the question of establishing a big cotton factory.

Measles continues to prevail in Washington township, near Batesville, Arkansas.

Last week, at San Antonio, Texas, Albert G. Hines was caught while burglarizing a boardinghouse.

The graves of the Confederate dead at Yazoo, Mississippi, will be decorated on the fourteenth instant.

At Augusta, Arkansas, last Thursday, the residence of W. P. Campbell was partially destroyed by fire. Loss, $700.

Last Tuesday, at Collierville, Tennessee, Miss Jennie B. Plummer had her arm broken by being thrown from a swing.

Burglaries entered and robbed the residence of Mrs. L. Bowles of a lot of goods at Grenada, Mississippi, last Friday night.

The residence of Wm. H. Finnegan, at Mississippi City, was destroyed by fire last week. Loss, $2000. Cause of fire accidental.

Last week the residence, corn-crib, smokehouse and outbuildings of Christopher Smith, near Grenada, Mississippi, were destroyed by fire.

Near Pine Bluff, Arkansas, last Thursday, John Dellman, while hunting, was shot and dangerously wounded by the accidental discharge of a shotgun in the hands of Adolph Bernalte.

Last week, near Pine Bluff, Arkansas, a little negro boy accidentally set fire to Roland Jones's cotton gin. It was destroyed, as was also eight bales of cotton. Loss, $800; no insurance.

Near White Church, J. S. Adams carried off the wife, wagon and yoke of steers belonging to one M. P. Adams, and leaving his wife and family. J. S. was the father of M. P. Adams.

In the Blackburn precinct, near Florence, Alabama, Mrs. Henry Hines was burned to death, her clothing catching fire while she was cooking. She was twenty years of age, and had been married but a few months.

The stock of goods of S. Lichtenstein & Co., of Grenada, Mississippi, which goods had been attached by creditors, was sold by the sheriff last week for $25,000 to other merchants of the city. The goods originally cost $45,000.

Near Sherman, Texas, recently, Frank Ray and Maxwell Smith were arrested on charges of attempting to commit outrages on little girls. The citizens were so excited over the affair that the prisoners had to be removed to keep them from being lynchbed.

At Whiteside Station on the Nashville and Chattanooga, Tennessee, while attempting to jump from a moving car fell back and had his arm cut off between the hand and elbow. He is sixty-two years of age.

The authorities at Hot Springs are considering the questions whether or not to permit Johnny Thompson to open a variety show in that city and also to permit Kate Merritt, of Little Rock, to open up a bagnio. The great moral question will be settled in a few days.

At Teon's Station, Tennessee, last week, Johnny Gallinus, a negro, murdered his wife, from whom he had been separated for two years, but whom he compelled to give up money when she had saved it. He broke in the door to her room and stabbed her to the heart with a knife.

At Pascagoula, Mississippi, during the past week, a dead negro was found on the river. The Austrian bark Tevere was destroyed by fire in the bay. She was laden with timber and was valued at $11,000. Thomas Percy cut with a knife William Thompson in the left side and shoulder, infiltrating serious wounds. Josephus Sporenburg was killed by a knife and the young men from Mobile whipped a negro and Ed Bielock cowhidled a negro who had insulted him. Pascagoula is becoming a city in a rapid manner, judging from the above indications of advanced civilization.

At Marshall, Texas, last week, W. T. Taylor, formerly of Marshall county, Alabama, shot and killed W. B. Alford. The latter had been drinking and punched some holes in Taylor's hat with a pocket-knife. The latter demonstrated, shook Alford roughly and slapped him in the face. Alford got a pistol, and meeting Taylor in the street and shouted, "Shut up!" and mediately fired at him. Taylor returned the fire once and stepped into Deckert's jewelry store, when the fire was continued through the window, each party firing four shots. Taylor's last shot killed Alford, the ball entering his forehead between the eyes. Taylor's cheek was slightly cut by a knife. Taylor was admitted to bail in the sun of $2000. Both combatants were young men and highly respected.
